These advancements enable the rigorous assessment of sapphire's performance as a substrate for superconducting qubits and a housing medium for ultra-long-lived qubits and microwave memories operating in the ultra-high-frequency quantum domain. This study investigates the impact of optical forces on the orbital characteristics of dielectric and metallic nanoparticles within a standing optical wave. Specifically, we examine the orbital damped oscillations of the particle and identify an energy dissipation mechanism. Notably, we discover an unconventional drag force acting on the particle, which is proportional to the square of its orbital velocity and acts in the opposite direction to its orbital angular momentum. This atypical force arises from second-harmonic radiation, which carries away angular momentum. Furthermore, we outline strategies to counteract this optical drag by implementing controlled lateral vibrations, and we highlight potential applications of this phenomenon in the field of optomechanics.

This study addresses a specific class of two-stage robust optimization problems characterized by binary uncertainty sets. By applying the Lagrangian dual method, we transform this into an equivalent problem that combines a mixed-integer linear program with a polyhedral cone constraint. We then resolve this reformulated problem by first constructing a relaxation and subsequently deriving an upper bound on the optimal value of its linear relaxation. Utilizing branch-and-bound techniques on this relaxed version allows us to generate high-quality feasible solutions for the original model. Finally, we present numerical experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

The proliferation of heterogeneous data sources has created a compelling need for effective multi-source data fusion and mining techniques. To address this, we introduce H4M, a dataset designed around four Beijing public datasets: BeijingTraffic, BeijingBus, BeijingWeather, and BeijingEdu. These sources encompass diverse modalities—including numerical, categorical, and textual data—and span four distinct domains: transportation, meteorology, education, and urban management. Characterized by high heterogeneity, complexity, and real-world variability, this collection facilitates the development of robust socioeconomic analytics methods. To the best of our knowledge, H4M represents the most comprehensive resource tailored for multi-source data fusion and mining research. To support such research, we have developed a dedicated Python library, named H4M-Tool, which facilitates seamless integration of these datasets and enables their analysis. This resource is made publicly available at https://github.com/THU-DMLT/H4M.

This work introduces a visual design-driven approach for exploring large-scale datasets. The method begins by converting data into images using a set of designs; subsequently, it maps the similarity space of datasets onto a low-dimensional surface through a self-organizing map (SOM). Users can then directly navigate this layout by specifying desired design-based attributes to filter and locate relevant data. We implemented the approach to create a design-oriented big data explorer, evaluating its efficacy via a study that yielded positive feedback on its efficiency and interactive capability.

In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have garnered significant attention for their capacity to effectively extract features from graph-structured data. Despite this, training GNNs remains costly due to the high computational resources required. In response, researchers have turned toward transfer learning to mitigate these challenges. Building on the successful application of this paradigm in other domains, this work investigates how transfer learning can enhance GNN training. We examine both inductive and transductive settings, analyzing how to transfer knowledge from a source task to a target task. Through a thorough analysis of existing literature, we outline the strengths and limitations of current approaches. Furthermore, we validate our findings through experiments on two newly proposed benchmarks, covering both inductive and transductive scenarios. Our results demonstrate that transfer learning yields substantial performance gains over training from scratch, thereby confirming its promising future in GNN research.

Set separation involves creating a mapping from an input set into a binary output space such that the distance in Hamming space between the image of a set and any specified query vector is at least a predefined threshold. This concept is fundamental to various areas, including set packing, set covering, and data streaming. This paper introduces a novel, elementary, combinatorial method to establish stronger and more numerous separation results. Additionally, it provides a randomized streaming algorithm capable of constructing such separating mappings. This approach achieves the optimal $O(\log n)$ space complexity for the $\alpha$-strong set separation variant with a parameter $\alpha \ge 1.5$.

The spin susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets across both classical and quantum regimes consistently exhibits Heisenberg-type non-analytic momentum behavior in their paramagnetic phase, regardless of the specific value of the spin $S$. When incorporated into the functional renormalization group (FRG) framework, this specific momentum dependence induces distinct non-analytic terms within the FRG flow equations. Consequently, these terms influence critical behavior and critical exponents, leading to a systematic and predictable modification of the standard Wilson-Fisher universality class.

Integrated photonics enables the generation of high-quality single photons, yet trapping and manipulating individual atoms presents significant challenges. This architecture facilitates the creation of single photons via excited atom-photon coupling through the integrated gratings, while simultaneously using a second grating to capture and control the atomic ground states. Our experiments demonstrate stable long-term operation, with atom-photon interactions persisting for over 10 minutes.

This work introduces the ZNN framework through a specialized problem of solving linear systems with time-varying coefficients, a task accomplished by formulating the system's evolution as dynamic differential equations. By applying algebra to these dynamics, the approach derives two types of solutions: one for the initial state and another for the evolution over time. These results are then leveraged to restructure existing Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNNs) so they can resolve this specific class of time-varying matrix problems. The analysis concludes with an examination of the convergence behavior of these ZNN implementations.

Although deep learning has become a dominant force in image classification, its reliance on vast datasets and its susceptibility to adversarial examples remain critical weaknesses. This paper introduces an alternative approach that leverages on-off center-surround fields for precise and resilient classification. By utilizing difference images to capture central features while ignoring peripheral noise, this method enables robust classification with significantly fewer training samples than traditional deep learning. Implemented as a binary classification model, it employs sigmoid activation to produce distinct outputs for center (focused) and surround (blurred) pathways. These outputs are categorized as "on" or "off" states, which serve as inputs to an on-off center-surround field layer, ultimately generating the final classification. Experimental results confirm that this architecture not only withstands attacks by noisy pixel perturbations and adversarial examples but also delivers superior performance compared to established deep learning models.

This study examines techniques for improving X-ray imaging systems that utilize elliptical or paraboloidal mirrors to achieve wide-field coverage. It outlines a general approach for determining mirror shapes and orientation based on specified requirements for field of view, magnification, and image quality. Additionally, the investigation explores methods to boost performance through active or passive mirror figure adjustments optimized for a specific focal scenario, refining mirror alignment and shape via a polynomial model, and utilizing a genetic algorithm to identify optimal configurations for a defined set of requirements.

We investigate the magnetic Bloch theorem and its consequences in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to a uniform perpendicular flux, specifically at the $2\pi$ flux condition where the magnetic unit cell encompasses two original cells. Utilizing the Bloch basis within a minimal model, we derive the magnetic Hofstadter butterfly, observing reentrant flat bands at high flux values. Furthermore, by examining the momentum-space analytic forms of eigenstates, we map out the Chern numbers across the entire Brillouin zone.

This paper introduces a method for rendering steganographic messages hidden within plain text using Long Short-Term Memory networks trained on existing plain-text and hidden-text pairs. Our approach achieves an accuracy rate exceeding 99.5% for 99.99% of the text while adapting to a wide range of base languages and encryption techniques without fine-tuning.

This paper describes a method that leverages Long Short-Term Memory networks trained on steganographic and plaintext pairs to generate steganographic content. Our system operates with over 99.5% accuracy for 99.99% of the text while accommodating various base languages and encryption schemes without fine-tuning, maintaining more than 99.5% accuracy for 99.99% of the text and supporting a variety of base languages and encryption techniques without fine-tuning.

Unit commitment (UC) is a critical process in power systems that determines the optimal generator on/off status over a forecast horizon to minimize operational expenses. Solving UC effectively requires accurately modeling generator costs and ramping rates, yet these parameters are often imprecise or unavailable in real-world scenarios. This uncertainty can result in suboptimal or infeasible UC decisions. To mitigate this, the authors introduce a cost modeling approach designed to identify the most probable cost and ramping rate profiles for a given generator. By evaluating cost models across diverse scenarios and solving the UC problem under uncertainty, decision-makers can select plans that remain robust and viable regardless of actual cost variations. Specifically, this study employs the Random Forest learning algorithm to derive the most plausible cost models, while a Monte Carlo framework assesses scenario variability and calculates cost-weighted constraint violation probabilities. These probabilities guide the selection of an appropriate cost model for each generator. Finally, probabilistic UC formulations are solved to generate solutions that explicitly account for uncertainty in cost models and constraints.

We report on the magnetic properties of the Kitaev candidate material $\alpha$-Li$_{2}$IrO$_{3}$ under applied pressure. High-field magnetization measurements indicate that pressure suppresses the long-range Néel antiferromagnetic order, with a complete transition to a dimer state occurring at approximately $p \approx 1.5$ GPa. Furthermore, neutron diffraction data confirm the persistence of hexagonally ordered magnetic moments up to 1.5 GPa, even as the Néel temperature drops to zero. These findings demonstrate that $\alpha$-Li$_{2}$IrO$_{3}$ is the first identified system where pressure successfully suppresses magnetic order to reach a Kitaev state. Additionally, the results offer valuable insights for investigating how spin-orbit coupling and bond frustration influence the phase diagram of Kitaev systems.

Synthetic Control Method (SCM) is a widely used approach to estimate treatment effects in policy analyses. This paper introduces a refined SCM framework, designated as TIISSC (The Identification and Inference for Synthetic SCM), which addresses specific limitations of the standard SCM theory. By utilizing TIISSC, researchers can derive more precise and accurate inferences regarding treatment effects. Drawing from the nearby causal inference framework, TIISSC offers a fresh theoretical perspective on SCM that overcomes the drawbacks associated with earlier SCM applications. Key enhancements in TIISSC include: (1) the capability to incorporate multiple treated units; (2) a relaxed assumption concerning the behavior of weight distributions as time progresses; (3) the inclusion of covariates and heterogeneous treatment effects within the analysis; and () the integration of covariate balancing power transformations into SCM, with corresponding adjustments to the TIISSC methodology. Empirical validation is provided through simulations and applications to real-world data, specifically examining the effects of the Affordable Care Act.

The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance serves as a powerful tool for measuring structural dissimilarity between graphs, with its applications spanning graph classification, clustering, and distance learning. Although effective, GW poses significant challenges: it necessitates the exchange of sensitive data, is unsuitable for privacy-preserving scenarios, and proves computationally prohibitive for massive datasets. This paper introduces a method to perform privacy-preserving GW distance computation on the implicit representation of graphs, enabling the analysis of distributed topological structures without revealing raw data. Our approach leverages the observation that GW distance can be decomposed into independent subtasks, each solvable via the $k$-means algorithm. By applying the distributed, differential privacy-enhanced $k$-means technique to these subtasks, the method facilitates the calculation of GW distance while ensuring local privacy for both the graph's topology and attributes. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to the specific privacy requirements of each participant in a distributed setting. We validate the method on the standard benchmark of distributed topological graphs, demonstrating that the computed GW distances remain indistinguishable from non-private benchmarks, while simultaneously providing robust protection for sensitive information.

We examine the impact of varying the polarization of a self-steepening laser pulse on electron injection and acceleration within a magnetized, collisional plasma. Our findings indicate that when using a linearly polarized pulse, the self-generated magnetic field is oriented parallel to the laser's propagation axis. In contrast, employing a circularly polarized pulse aligns this field perpendicularly to the laser's polarization direction. This field orientation significantly influences collisional electron scattering and ohmic losses. Specifically, when the field is parallel to the laser beam, collisions and losses are minimized, whereas they are intensified when the field is perpendicular. These results demonstrate that the self-generated magnetic field can be effectively controlled by selecting the polarization state of the incident laser pulse, thereby optimizing injection and acceleration efficiency.

This study examines the feasibility of investigating double beta decay alongside dark matter-induced single nucleon processes in $^{194}$Pt. We employ a relativistic energy density functional to derive point-proton and neutron densities, which subsequently inform the selection of optimal impurity concentrations for a platinum-based double beta decay detector. Furthermore, we assess whether such a system could effectively probe dark matter interactions. Although $^{194}$Pt is not yet a double beta decay candidate, we anticipate that a dedicated experiment could achieve sensitivity comparable to current benchmarks for the half-life of $^{194}$Pt $\to$ $^{190}$Pd $+ 2e^-$ and for dark matter searches within the sub-GeV regime.

To achieve high-performance prediction, Unobtainable Transit (UbT) specifies a per-stop, per-minute request rate for historical data. However, because data availability is fragmented and irregular, collecting a complete dataset is often unfeasible. To address this, we present a deep learning strategy using both Transformer and Long Short-Term Network (LSTM) architectures to forecast missing values. Experiments indicate that this approach yields negligible mean squared error (MSE) and maintains minimal model complexity. The study concludes by evaluating how this preprocessed dataset impacts downstream forecasting performance.

Few-shot learning seeks to create models capable of classifying new data with limited examples. This study introduces a new approach that constructs prototypes for each class by integrating information from both the support and query sets. The method's effectiveness is verified through extensive testing on standard few-shot learning benchmarks, including miniImagenet, CUB, and Stanford Cars. The results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods by a significant margin.

This work establishes a general proof of a theorem, demonstrating that any stable state breaking a persistent non-invertible symmetry must be spontaneous in nature. While tailored specifically to any charge conserved under such a symmetry—such as charge $Q$ under a charge conservation that does not involve symmetry breaking—the implications of this result are far-reaching. Specifically, the theory predicts that any phase preserving the charge $Q$ under a charge conservation that does not involve symmetry breaking must also spontaneously break the symmetry. This result has significant consequences for understanding how matter behaves under various symmetries, including those associated with charge conservation without symmetry breaking. In conclusion, the study provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing how to preserve and spontaneously break charges under non-invertible symmetry conditions.

A graph is semi-transitive precisely when it is transitive and all its induced subgraphs are either transitive or independent. A directed graph is defined as semi-transitive if its underlying undirected form qualifies as such. Examples of graphs that are both simple and semi-transitive include paths, cycles, and split graphs. Split graphs are characterized by a partition of their vertices into two sets: a clique, where all members are mutually connected, and an independent set with no internal connections. This study examines the conditions under which a split graph can be semi-transitive in its directed form. Specifically, this involves identifying the requirements for the adjacency directions between the two vertex subsets to satisfy semi-transitivity criteria. Consequently, this analysis yields a new characterization of semi-transitive split graphs, a structure that is notably prevalent in various scientific fields.

Identification capabilities for purely hadronic $\tau$ decays, specifically the $\tau^+ \to ^{+} + \nu_\tau$ channel, have been assessed using data from the $\ppbar$ collider at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC. By training and applying a deep neural network to isolate these $\tau$ leptons from background events, the analysis achieved an efficiency of 70% with a signal-to-background ratio of 1.5. This performance represents a substantial enhancement over the standard identification methods employed by the CMS detector.

As data sets continue to expand in size, they increasingly demand the use of machine learning for efficient classification. Although Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have been established as a robust probabilistic framework for prediction, their application in this field remains underutilized. This study investigates BNNs specifically for classification tasks within massive, high-dimensional datasets, such as the one provided by the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST-BOSS). Utilizing the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (LSST-BO subset) data to categorize galaxies and quasars, we demonstrate that BNNs achieve performance comparable to standard feedforward neural networks (FFNNs) regarding accuracy. Furthermore, we illustrate that BNNs generate reliable estimates of expected classification error and deliver trustworthy measures of uncertainty for individual predictions.

This study presents a coupled-wave model for intermodal Brillouin scattering in photonic lattice fibers, applicable to both step-index and air-silica composite structures. The model accounts for couplings between longitudinal Brillouin wavevectors, Brillouin frequency, and the phase-matching conditions between optical and acoustic modes. Employing full-scale molecular dynamics simulations, the acoustic mode structure of the fiber lattice was determined. Consequently, intermodal Brillouin coupling strengths were calculated across various modal configurations, with phase-matching constraints mapped into a mode diagram. The findings highlight that intermodal Brillouin interactions are particularly significant in the low-order modal spectrum.

The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMP) are both NP-hard challenges prevalent in data mining and operations research. This study examines SUKP and BMP within a specific context where the knapsack capacity is small, a condition that enables the derivation of a specific polynomial-time exact algorithm. Additionally, we develop a set of local search approaches designed to tackle these problems efficiently. Experimental results indicate that a newly proposed hybrid approach outperforms state-of-the-art heuristics, delivering superior solution qualities in a remarkably short timeframe.

Churn constitutes a significant issue across numerous industries, particularly within the highly competitive gambling sector, where understanding player attrition is vital for sustaining engagement. This study presents an innovative approach to churn prediction by integrating online activity logs with self-conducted surveys. The research employs a machine learning framework to forecast the likelihood of cessation and pinpoints specific feature values that most significantly influence this outcome. Additionally, the authors outline the characteristics of those likely to leave in the near future, offering actionable strategic insights. The findings suggest that combining survey and activity data substantially enhances predictive accuracy compared to models relying solely on activity data. Ultimately, these results provide gambling operators with a robust framework to develop data-driven initiatives for retaining users.

The calculation of the twist-2 distribution function is performed via standard lattice QCD methods, while the ratio between distributions is determined through perturbation theory. The resulting TMDPDF formula is valid for both light and hard gluons, accommodating any value of x and the Q scale, provided the impact parameter is fixed.

Quantum electrodynamics calculations demonstrate that electromagnetic interactions involving low-momentum virtual photons and atomic nuclei within ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions yield ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collision (UPC) cross sections. These interactions produce final states with significant transverse momentum, including single or multiple pairs of lepton pairs, as well as hadronic systems such as $\rho$, $\phi$, $J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$, and multi-hadron configurations. The analysis reveals that these mechanisms are most effective in ultra-relativistic UPCs at energies comparable to those at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), where they dominate over other processes. The study concludes by evaluating the influence of these contributions on various LHC experiments.

This work introduces a context-aware, video-based risk measurement system designed to quantify cyclist danger levels using video footage from standard 1080p consumer cameras. Our method estimates proximity distances based on visual cues from widely available consumer devices operating at 1080p resolution.

This study presents a barrier-based approach to guarantee safety secureness in motion planning for systems subjected to disturbances and modeling inaccuracies. By leveraging Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), we define a safe set that the system is guaranteed not to exit despite external disturbances and parameter uncertainties. To integrate these safety guarantees into motion planning, we introduce a new cost term into Model Predictive Control (MPC), which ensures that trajectories remain within the CBF-defined safe region under both nominal conditions and during disturbances. The method's efficacy in robustly planning safe trajectories is validated through simulation studies involving a drone operating under disturbance and uncertainty.

An element $x$ in a ring $R$ is defined as primitive if it is not a zero divisor and not a unit. The enveloping number of $R$, denoted by $E(R)$, represents the total count of such primitive elements within the structure. In the course of this paper, we have determined the necessary conditions under which $R$ satisfies $E(R)=1$, $2$, or an even integer. Additionally, the text provides a formula for calculating $E(R)$ specifically for chains of rings and an explicit formula for the case where $R$ is a direct product of two rings.

Adversarial examples represent a significant threat to artificial intelligence systems, yet current defense strategies often rely on non-natural methods that can compromise model accuracy for the sake of resilience. This paper introduces a novel approach to achieve robustness against adversarial attacks, resulting in a more inherent resistance without sacrificing performance. The core methodology involves a streamlined training protocol that integrates knowledge distillation with adversarial training. Additionally, we evaluate these models against a broader spectrum of attack methodologies, including previously untested variants. Empirical results indicate that this framework not only confers stronger resilience but also enhances accuracy for a specific class of attacks.

This study examines a specific class of nonlocal traffic models defined by a general function $f$ and its corresponding convex relaxation model, denoted as $F$. By implementing a singular perturbation approach, the nonlocal formulation is approximated through a local model. The analysis establishes that entropy-admissible solutions of the local system also satisfy the nonlocal system in the general setting, with a singular layer of complexity emerging in $t$ dependent solely on the properties of $F$. The study further proves the existence of a unique, globally convergent solution toward equilibrium within an $L^{\infty}$ framework, with the convergence rate determined solely by the properties of $F$. The final section provides numerical simulations to validate these findings and demonstrate their practical application.

The brain constitutes a complex network of neurons and synapses that facilitate information transmission among various regions. To comprehend the underlying mechanisms of human cognition, it is essential to investigate the connectivity between these areas. We propose a novel methodology for analyzing the brain's functional architecture by modeling regional blood flow dynamics as a continuous Gaussian graphical network. This approach utilizes an information-theoretic metric called Total Correlation (TC) to quantify the integration of brain functional connectivity. TC effectively captures the degree of interdependence among different brain areas, thereby serving as a robust indicator of global neural integration.

To validate this framework, we conducted an empirical study using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from 1,108 individuals in the UK Bioback repository. Our results demonstrate a robust positive correlation between TC-derived connectivity strength and comprehensive cognitive assessments, including the Global Assessment of Cognition (GCAI), cognitive performance scores, and memory evaluations. Furthermore, this large-scale correlation analysis validates our findings by revealing that individual differences in global brain integration are strongly associated with variations in cognitive abilities.

This study introduces a Clifford algebra framework for the Segal-Bargmann transform. We define transform transformations that map Clifford algebra-valued entire functions, which are Taylor-isomorphic to Clifford algebra-valued functions defined on specific classifying spaces. Within this setup, transform segments serve as the generalization of standard Hilbert space transforms to Clifford algebra settings. These transforms act as maps within the Taylor isomorphism class of specific functions. Furthermore, we establish that the transform segment corresponding to a specific structure is equivalent under Taylor isomorphism conditions. Finally, we introduce corresponding transform segments equipped with a specific metric structure and determine its associated properties.

We investigate how to condition a Gaussian field for a specific path segment, ensuring the resulting conditional field remains within the same class of models. Achieving this generally requires increasing the complexity of the Gaussian field by a factor of $d+1$. We provide an algorithm to construct such a construction and prove that, in the condition where the path is piecewise $C^1$, the field's sample paths possess the required additional dimension. We also show that the resulting condition requires only a linear increase in the number of parameters. Finally, we provide an example of how to apply the method to the case of the Brownian motion.

This study explores the deployment of a hybrid sensor network combining terrestrial nodes with aerial drones. We introduce a model for an on-the-fly dynamic network formed when a drone carries a specific number of batteries, allowing it to act as a relay between ground sensors and the network. The primary objective is to maximize the coverage area. The model accounts for the battery consumption caused by both carrying the extra mass and the process of wireless link establishment. The research establishes key analytical results, including the specific conditions under which wireless connections are used and the impact of battery levels on network topology. The paper also presents simulation results to validate these findings.

The Long-Baseline Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is designed to investigate neutrino oscillations with unprecedented precision, utilizing a massive 70-kiloton liquid argon time-projection chamber situated approximately 1,100 kilometers underground in the D'Agostino Hall complex. This distance, part of the Deep Subterranean Neutrino Experiment, is intended to shield the detector from atmospheric neutrino backgrounds. By analyzing a neutrino beam generated 1,000 kilometers away at Fermilab, the experiment will observe oscillation-driven effects with high sensitivity. Key research objectives include determining the neutrino mass hierarchy, measuring CP violation to probe baryogenesis origins, precisely constraining $\theta_{13}$, observing oscillation patterns via the Earth's crust, and studying oscillation behavior in the Earth's mantle.

The presence of heavy particles, such as heavy resonant top quarks, can be identified through signatures involving many jets within collider events. To optimize the observability of these heavy particles, we refine our standard top quark identification capabilities by examining how specific features contribute to our classification performance. Employing the probabilistic SHapley Additive exPost facto (SHAP) method, we quantify the importance of features within our discrimination variables. This analysis reveals that while our original top tags rely heavily on subjets originating from bottom quarks, refined tagging strategies prioritize different variables to further boost efficiency. We validate these findings using both simulated datasets and those from the Large Hadron Collider Run 2. Furthermore, to assess how our improved top detectors perform in searching for supersymmetry, we examine their utility in interpreting results from the gluino decay analysis into two top quarks.

In Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), the experience replay (ER) strategy is widely employed to enhance sample efficiency and training stability. However, a critical limitation remains: interactions with the environment are often discarded after a single use, causing the variance associated with individual samples to diminish inefficiently. To address this, we introduce an updated ER mechanism that reduces overall variance by reusing experiences multiple times. By leveraging a first-order optimization approach, the method iteratively refines the update direction to further lower variance. Extensive experiments across four continuous control tasks in the OpenAI Gym framework demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior sample efficiency and performance compared to both the baseline PERL and other existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

This work offers a detailed, step-by-step analysis of the computational similarities and differences between the Hubbard-Stratonovich (H-S) transformation and the superbosonization (SB) equation, a method used to linearize four-fermion interactions in quantum field theory. Both techniques transform systems containing interacting fermions into those featuring an effective bosonic sector for easier analysis. While the H-S employs a path integral over a new auxiliary variable to factorize a quadratic fermionic term into a product of bilinears, the SB equation achieves the same linearization but expressed in terms of generating functions and correlation functions of the resulting bosonic fields. Additionally, a detailed analysis of the loop expansion for both methods reveals that their coupling constants and momentum-mapping schemes are intimately connected.

Human motion is a fundamental form of communication, and accurately forecasting its trajectory is crucial for various computer vision and robotics applications. However, current methods often struggle with limited accuracy regarding specific, fine-grained aspects of movement. This paper introduces MoDeRNN, a new approach for spatiotemporal prediction that achieves higher fidelity regarding human motion characteristics by extracting key features from skeleton data. Our methodology models the movement in two complementary dimensions: the temporal evolution of joint positions and the specific velocities of individual joints. By capturing this dual perspective, the system significantly improves prediction fidelity. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing techniques in effectively anticipating essential characteristics of human motion.

This paper introduces Josephine, a JavaScript-Rust hybrid runtime that addresses the limitations of existing web assembly frameworks. Current approaches either lack mature support for extensive web APIs or struggle with performance due to their web-centric designs. Josephine resolves this by leveraging WebAssembly modules that auto-manage memory, eliminating the need for Rust developers to explicitly handle lifetimes. By leveraging this capability, it bypasses core obstacles preventing JavaSCript applications from securely utilizing Rust, a language currently underserved on the web.

Majorana dark matter and neutrinoless double-beta decay are often considered the primary frameworks for understanding lepton number violation. While these phenomena are traditionally studied separately, this study explores the possibility of their interplay within a single majorana model. We demonstrate that the nature of the produced dark matter directly influences the decay signatures, leading to novel experimental approaches for detecting lepton number violation. Furthermore, these findings suggest a new avenue for investigating lepton number breaking at high-energy colliders.

This paper introduces a method for BP list decoding that leverages polar subcodes. The proposed approach establishes a suboptimal decoding framework that permits errors within the subcode, thereby enhancing performance compared to optimal subcode decoding while maintaining a tractable, efficient procedure. The study provides a non-asymptotic analysis of the method, demonstrating that its performance is bounded below by BP decoding applied to the subject's subcode, which itself performs at a level comparable to a message-passing Belief Propagation decoder. When two objects with distinct point-spread functions (PSFs) are superimposed, a common assumption mistakenly equates the resulting composite PSF with a simple convolution of their individual functions. It further demonstrates that, under the limit of infinitesimal sampling, the functions always commute.

Fracture in crystals is modeled as a sequence of successive atomic bond ruptures, where the overall process is governed by the weakest bond within a specific volume. This least-resistant bond is identified using a Monte Carlo simulation of atomic vibrations, treating each bond's resistance as a random variable following a Gaussian distribution. Consequently, the calculated fracture strength for various materials is directly proportional to their bulk modulus, with results for specific substances aligning closely with experimental data.

This work examines the coupling of chordal Brownian motion with multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) and its interaction with two types of Gaussian free fields (GFF): the logarithmic-mirrored GFF and the square-root-coupled GFF. Additionally, we demonstrate that the level-set of the log-GFF corresponds to a SLE with sides, and the level-set of the square-root GFF as a SLE with multi-sides where the boundary conditions are specific to the log-Gaussian model. Blockchain technology has garnered significant attention for its potential to foster trust and security in data storage and processing, making it an ideal fit for applications like IoT. Despite this, the integration of IoT with blockchain faces challenges primarily due to a lack of specialized frameworks. This paper introduces a new blockchain-driven framework designed to enhance security and trustworthiness in IoT environments. The authors detail the specific modifications required to build such a framework and validate its efficacy through a food supply chain use case.

Cell morphology is determined by the dynamic equilibrium between intracellular forces and the mechanical properties of the cortex, representing a vital area of study in cellular biology and biophysics. While statistical models of cell shapes have been developed to detect anomalies indicative of disease, topological approaches often fail to capture the continuous nature of shape variations driven by dynamic processes. To address this, we present a approach that not only generates realistic cell shapes but also creates their corresponding force fields. Our method utilizes vector fields derived from implicit functions, which offer a compact representation and facilitate topological manipulation. Specifically, we employ a variational framework based on a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a continuous latent space for shape generation. Concurrently, we apply a conditional variational approach to produce force fields corresponding to specific shapes. Our experiments demonstrate that the resulting cells exhibit high fidelity to experimental data, with the associated force fields offering new insights into cellular dynamics.

This research investigates how individuals with disabilities dependent on printing assistive technologies can access printed materials. Through interviews with users of Braille display devices and software, the authors identified key obstacles preventing access to printed resources for those who cannot read standard print. Additionally, the study introduces a new metric for document navigability by analyzing the structural attributes of file content. The authors propose a method to evaluate navigability scores and demonstrate how this model can guide document creators in making materials more user-friendly for people who rely on Braille displays.

We introduce a new generation of deep language representations derived through generalized autoregressive pre-training. Our methodology incorporates the Parallel Sentence Prediction task, which enables the model to anticipate the structural configuration of data samples. This technique is applied within the Transformer XL architecture, an extension of the Transformer model that utilizes relative positional encodings to capture long-range sequence dependencies. To further enhance the model's robustness and performance, we incorporate bidirectional context during the pre-training phase. Empirical results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses GPT and BERT, achieving state-of-the-art results on eight different datasets.

Stellar activity can mimic or mask atmospheric signatures in exoplanet transit spectra, a challenge that is particularly acute for low-resolution (LR) observations of small planets. We investigate whether high-resolution (HR) cross-correlation techniques can reduce activity-induced noise to the same extent as traditional modeling applied to low-resolution data. Using Kepler-444b as a case study, we simulated stellar activity by injecting spectral lines from solar spots and plages into solar data, which we then modeled as planetary atmospheres. We compared the results by running both traditional modeling on the simulated LR data and high-fidelity activity subtraction on the simulated HR data. Our findings indicate that while modeling successfully recovers the signal in LR data, a high-fidelity modeling approach is superior for recovering signals in HR data. We conclude that HR cross-correlation does not mitigate stellar activity effectively; instead, precise modeling remains necessary. This underscores the importance of obtaining precise stellar activity data and developing robust stellar activity models, especially when analyzing small planets.

Centipedes of the genus Scolopendra possess remarkable abilities to traverse various terrains, including vertical walls and ceilings. This study investigates their mechanics for surface swimming on calm water. We present a biomechanical model that accounts for the specific physical properties of centipedes, including their light body mass, elongated shape, and the air layer that adheres to their cuticle. Our findings indicate that centipedes move by propelling themselves through the propulsion of this trapped air, while the hydrophobic nature of their legs and setae enhances mobility by facilitating gliding and reducing hydrodynamic drag. Additionally, we examine the specific biomechanics of the first and last leg pairs, noting that the leading pair generates most of the propulsive force, whereas the trailing pair acts primarily to steer the body.

Hydrodynamic models are essential tools for simulating the propagation of tsunami waves generated by space impacts. These models are typically validated using benchmark problems with known analytical solutions, though this validation becomes insufficient for the extreme, dispersive regimes anticipated in the near-Earth environment. Consequently, this study conducts a benchmark assessment of seven leading hydrodynamic simulators in an inshore dispersive scenario to evaluate their reliability for future adaptive modeling of asteroid-induced tsunamis.

The discovery of infrared-luminous, optically dark galaxies (IUDGs) has been a persistent mystery, yet the recent findings of JWST have significantly advanced our understanding of them. Additionally, we have measured their redshifts, finding that the mean value is $z=1.72 \pm 0.17$, with a distribution that spans from $z=0.7$ to $z=3.3$. By combining these findings with a comprehensive multi-wavelength dataset, we have successfully modeled their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to derive key physical properties, including their star formation histories, dust content, and star formation rates. Our analysis indicates that these high-luminosity IUDGs are dominated by dust-obscured star formation. Furthermore, by comparing this sample to a control group of luminous, infrared-bright galaxies, we observed that the IUDGs exhibit significantly lower star formation efficiencies.

This study examines the distinct impacts of distinct El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) flavors on global areas experiencing extreme seasonal precipitation—both very high and very low. We utilize a novel methodology to detect and quantify these effects, utilizing a 60-year (1950–2010) global precipitation dataset and classifying ENSO events into three clusters: the traditional, the 1990s, and the 2000s. While the overall precipitation response is consistent across all three flavors, the magnitude of these impacts varies significantly between them. We observe a differential pattern: the traditional cluster exerts the strongest influence on very low precipitation zones, whereas the 2000s cluster exerts the strongest influence on areas with very high precipitation.

Non-affine deformations are a defining feature of complex materials, including colloidal gels, glasses, and biological tissues. However, their characterization remains difficult because most experimental methods lack the spatial resolution required to capture the large-scale fluctuations of deformation. This work introduces a novel approach to detecting non-affine behavior by applying a technique that previously achieved nanoscale precision to system-wide light scattering events. By combining a laser-based gradient index with a numerical model that accounts for diffraction effects, we successfully measured non-affine growth in a three-dimensional colloidal gel.

This study examines a single-species dynamic model characterized by age-structured dynamics, environmental toxicity, and behavioral responses. Species distribution is segmented into susceptible and toxic groups; individuals transition from the susceptible to the toxic state through a density-dependent mechanism. The age-structured susceptible population adheres to a non-local reaction-diffusion framework, with the objective of identifying conditions ensuring the coexistence of all species groups. This analysis involves characterizing the steady-state profiles of multi-group reaction-diffusion systems. The core methodology relies on coupling the groups' non-local diffusion terms with group interaction equations, which are analyzed through spectral properties of a related operator family.

This paper examines a comprehensive class of axiomatic systems—specifically sequent and hypersequent calculus systems—understood as extensional axiomatizations of structural logic axioms via collections of structural rules termed "structural axioms." Unlike traditional approaches that rely on weakening and contraction rules, our framework utilizes corresponding axioms within a hypersequent context. We establish decidability for these calculi and analyze their complexity, specifically focusing on constant-depth hypersequents where depth remains bounded but height is not restricted. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of our method on non-constant depth hypersequents and demonstrate its applicability to several prominent examples, including transitivity, commutativity, and associativity.

Taxonomy Term Recommendation (TTR) aims to suggest unqueried term expansions based on user input, a capability vital for enhancing search utility across e-commerce and other critical domains. To address the limitations of existing methods, this work introduces a representation learning framework that models the input user query in hyperbolic space. This approach not only captures the semantic closeness of terms but also maintains the tree structure provided by the original taxonomy. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we utilize the Amazon dataset and evaluate our algorithm against current state-of-the-art solutions. The results indicate that our proposed method outperforms competing approaches in both accuracy and efficiency.

Furthermore, HF methods are shown to be unsuitable for modeling intermolecular forces, as the presence of an electric field introduces substantial errors in the resulting binding energy calculations.

Resilience, the capacity to withstand and bounce back from disruptions, is increasingly recognized as a critical factor in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). Residing at the intersection of engineering and the social sciences, the study of CPS resilience involves a multidisciplinary analysis of system behavior during and after cyber or physical disturbances. This research focuses on developing an STL-based model to address resilience within CPS. Furthermore, we incorporate a "response time" metric to quantify the minimum temporal gap required between guarantee and goal satisfaction, specifically when operating through a recovery strategy. To demonstrate this, we present a case study involving a resilient control system for an industrial robot.

This dataset covers a 2000 km² area in the western United States, comprising 1000 sites. Our analysis targets a search window of 20 days during the summer period to identify signals that may indicate the presence of such matter.

Quantitative Information Flow (QIF) is a domain within computer science focused on measuring the quantity of information leaked to adversaries through a system's outputs. This study presents a generalized framework for constructing HMMs that explicitly incorporates side-channel noise. Built upon the concepts of monads and comonads in category theory, this extended HMM formulation integrates the discrete probabilistic aspects of traditional Hidden Markov Models with continuous distributions, effectively bridging the gap between standard HMMs and generative models. This capability makes the framework particularly well-suited for modeling QIO scenarios. This work contributes a foundational theory supporting such models and provides a constructive method for building them, thereby establishing a solid basis for subsequent research in the modeling of these systems.

This work examines the nonlocal characteristics of the most probable, statistically steady states in one-dimensional Burgers turbulence subjected to periodic boundary conditions and linear dissipation. We demonstrate that, within the inviscid limit of vanishing dissipation, the local conservation of mass and momentum generates long-range correlations that determine the structure of the probability density function for the highest-order spatial derivatives of the velocity field. Specifically, these conservation laws restrict the spatial distribution of discontinuities to a finite set, thereby shaping the event's statistical profile. Furthermore, as the dissipative parameter decreases, the system exhibits an emergent, asymptotic dynamic consistency, which accounts for the alignment of high-order structures and influences the remaining statistical properties.

Scattering experiments serve as a vital tool for investigating new physics beyond the Standard Model. We introduce a new framework called the Flexible Scattering Phenomenology (FSP), designed to identify deviations from Standard Model predictions in scattering cross-sections. This approach utilizes a flexible functional form to model differential cross-sections, which are subsequently fitted against experimental data. By examining the goodness of fit, one can detect potential Standard Model violations. We demonstrate that FSP is a versatile method for identifying various Beyond Standard Model signatures, including contact interactions, resonances, and excited states. Additionally, we show its utility in pinpointing regions in parameter space that remain uncovered by existing analyses.

This work derives the free energy of blackbody radiation confined within parallel plates, incorporating corrections for how those plates influence each other via Casimir forces. Drawing from recent research (Phys. Rev. D 102, 024028 [2106.00286]) which provides a model for the spectral energy density of blackbody radiation in the presence of Casimir effects, we calculate the resulting thermodynamic potentials. These calculations demonstrate that when plate separations are sufficiently small, the internal energy, free energy, and pressure deviate from their standard forms described by Planck's law. We further explore the broader implications these findings have for the thermodynamics of black holes and the nature of Unruh radiation.

To protect user privacy, privacy-enhancing systems are increasingly being integrated into location-based services. Among these, $k$-anonymity is a well-known and frequently employed technique. This study introduces a new metric termed *conditional prior probability* (or conditional prior) specifically to measure the level of anonymity within location data sets. The proposed approach segments data sets into clusters, ensuring that each contains at least $k$ records with spatial proximity. By calculating the conditional prior probability for each pair of points within a group, the method determines the degree of spatial overlap. Ultimately, this metric facilitates a more robust and quantitative evaluation of spatial partitioning strategies and their associated anonymity guarantees.

Accurately and reliably localizing 3D LiDAR point clouds is crucial for autonomous systems operating in large outdoor environments. While the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) approach is a well-established global method, it suffers from a local-to-global ambiguity when multiple local minima exist. We introduce NDT-Transformer, a method that leverages self-attention to encode scene semantics and attention in cross-modal layers to align these semantic features with the target environment for robust target acquisition. We further demonstrate that this architecture can be trained in an end-to-end fashion to jointly optimize the global optimization strategy and parameters for point cloud registration. We have deployed our model on a large-scale dataset comprising 33.5 hours of data collected from 110 kilometers of driving routes. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves a 20% improvement in localization accuracy compared to baseline strategies relying solely on intensity data.

This research investigates the robustness and predictive capability of connectivity metrics derived from multisite functional MRI (fMRI) data. Using a dataset of 1,000 scans collected via the ENIGMA pipeline across 10 sites, we examined associations between these metrics and well-established biological and clinical factors, including age, sex, cognitive performance, and diagnosis. To address confounding factors such as scanner artifacts, we applied corrections for motion, spatial smoothing, and linear non-biological variance. We evaluated a range of metrics, including within-network power, between-network functional connectivity, graph-theoretic measures, and machine learning predictions. Our findings reveal that while within-network power remains significantly associated with motion levels, no other metric showed significant results after correction for motion and other covariates. Furthermore, while machine learning models could distinguish diagnostic groups, their performance did not reach statistical significance when evaluating interactions with motion, age, sex, or cognitive scores. We also observed that multisite functional connectivity predictions lacked stability across training and test datasets, indicating a failure to generalize. Ultimately, these results suggest that average functional connectivity metrics and predictive models based on them are unreliable for drawing robust inferences from multisite fMRI data.

This paper introduces a naming algorithm that is Beeping-Common and utilizes only one bit per node. The study also establishes a lower bound on the count of rounds necessary for network naming under these specific energy-saving constraints.

This study establishes a robust and versatile algorithm for evaluating 3D gravitational anomalies in GSU(N) theories, a family that encompasses almost all two-dimensional chiral gauge theories, alongside specific boundary conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these results are consistent with existing literature, and we briefly explore the application of this methodology to the phase diagram of 2D SU(N) Chern-Simons models.

This study examines the so-called "direct" method for investigating global solutions to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations across various function spaces. We establish that both subcritical and critical inhomogeneous essential Besov spaces \(\dot{B}_{p,q}^{-2+2/p}(\mathbb{R}^3)\), where \(1 < p < \infty\) and \(q = p\) or \(q = p-2\), are critical for these equations. This study examines the magnon spectrum and dynamic response of a one-dimensional antiferromagnetic system at finite temperature, revealing that intrinsically, a nonlinear spectral shift occurs to higher frequencies as we increase the system's temperature. Furthermore, thermal fluctuations cause the magnon spectrum to exhibit squeezing at both low- and high-energy frequencies, with the extent of this effect being significantly greater at the low-frequency range.

Code-based cryptosystems utilizing multidimensional (MD) codes face significant challenges due to the high computational complexity associated with converting between their multidimensional and vector-space representations. Our approach also includes a detailed security analysis and a comparison with Loidreau's original construction, demonstrating that the schemes maintain robust security comparable to previous efforts while eliminating the burden of complex data transformations.

This work proposes a novel approach to improve the MLM objective by leveraging a thesaurus to predict word relationships. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates multi-party collaboration on sensitive datasets without exposing the raw data. While VFL has been the focus of recent research, there is a notable lack of studies specifically targeting its security and privacy vulnerabilities. This paper introduces a novel VFL protocol and demonstrates that an adversary can compromise the privacy of participating parties, the integrity of the resulting model, and the data confidentiality through a malicious actor within the system. Unlike horizontal federated learning, the vertical context allows attackers to leverage specific data intersections to breach privacy with significantly fewer resources. We prove that even a partially malicious party with access to only a single communication channel in VFL poses substantial privacy risks. Our findings reveal that a sophisticated attacker can successfully launch a data inference attack to deduce private information and a model poisoning attack to corrupt VFL outcomes. We also provide a theoretical framework to analyze the privacy risks of VFL protocols and outline concrete countermeasures to address these threats.

Using light-cone sum rules (QCD LCSRs), we investigate the semileptonic decay process of a $B$-meson into a proton and a dark antibaryon. We derive the hadronic matrix element for the $B$ to p transition, extracting the corresponding form factors through a next-leading-order analysis of the $b$-quark-pair annihilation channel within the $B$-meson light-cone distribution amplitup (LCDAs). Our results indicate that the $B$-meson can decay into dark antibaryons, offering a viable mechanism for the production of these exotic states.

This paper introduces Intelligent City Defense Game, a framework designed to model resource allocation strategies for defending socio-cyber-physical cities against attacks. The city is represented as a graph where nodes signify districts and edges represent the communication links between them.

The relationship between the thermodynamic phase transition of a black hole situated within a finite-volume cavity and the geometry of an AdS space is examined. The analysis focuses on the implications of performing this transition between two topologically distinct manifolds, specifically changing the spatial geometry from an infinite plane to a 3-torus. The findings reveal that the nature of the transition changes: it becomes a smooth, second-order phase transition when the specific volume of the cavity is below a critical value, whereas an abrupt, first-order transition occurs above this critical volume threshold.

Neural models have recently emerged as a powerful approach for handling the challenge of identifying and treating with label noise in classification, though they often struggle with poor sample efficiency and difficulty generalizing to new domains. Evaluated on standard label noise benchmarks, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, it demonstrates efficient training with a limited number of clean labels and strong capability to adapt to fresh test data distributions.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction in various domains, yet their application is often hindered by a scarcity of labeled training data. The architecture utilizes a dual-branch design: one branch relies on the primary labeled dataset, while the other leverages the generated pseudo-labels. These branches are trained in an alternating fashion, with parameters updated based on their combined performance metrics. Extensive experiments across various graph datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing techniques.

Differentially private distributed machine learning (DPML) has recently emerged as a prominent research area, yet its application to tree-based models remains limited. Existing approaches for private decision trees either fail to guarantee differential privacy or struggle to scale effectively. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing two novel algorithms for building private decision trees that ensure strong differential privacy while maintaining scalability across large datasets. The first approach, a direct method, modifies the standard tree construction process to satisfy privacy constraints without compromising the core decision logic. The second is an indirect approach, which reformulates decision trees as piecewise constant functions; this allows the use of well-established methods for creating private regressors and polytopes. We rigorously prove that both methods provide strong differential privacy guarantees. Empirical evaluations on large-scale datasets demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art solutions for both regression and classification tasks while maintaining computational efficiency.

This study investigates a regularized form of Rényi divergence within an operator-based framework, which is widely applicable in machine learning scenarios. We propose a proximal gradient algorithm to solve this optimization task by leveraging Nesterov's accelerated gradient technique, and we derive specific algorithms for the squared L2-regularized case and the regularized squared L2 case. The former corresponds to finding projections onto a sublevel set defined by a convex loss, whereas the latter resembles computing the exponential family maximum likelihood estimator. We also present an alternative algorithm based on the more recent Tsallis-Bregman proximal operator. For this approach, we provide a tailored proximal procedure and a corresponding accelerated gradient algorithm. We further derive an algorithm specific to Gaussian exponential families and prove its convergence properties. Additionally, we validate the effectiveness of these methods through numerical experiments.

Traditional Bayesian best-subitive model selection typically relies on minimizing the posterior expected sum of squared errors within a fixed collection of models. However, when dealing with a potentially infinite sequence of nested models, this approach faces two main issues: the larger models often dominate the larger model collection, and the model averaging process is difficult to interpret. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a method for MAP (Model Averaging and Penalization) model selection that utilizes a specific penalty term. This penalty is derived from the Bayesian prior distribution and a carefully selected set of models, with the aim of approximating a broader pool of best models rather than a specific one. In the context of chain event graph (ChEV) data, this proposed technique outperforms conventional approaches, as shown by its superior ability to select appropriate models.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of damped inertial dynamics equipped with Tikhonov regularization for solving an operator equation involving a second-order operator. It is demonstrated that if the regularization parameter vanishes at an appropriate rate relative to the time variable, the dynamics converge strongly to the smallest norm solution of said equation. Furthermore, we establish that by employing a specific choice of weight functions within the regularization term, the rate of this convergence can be significantly enhanced. These results also hold for the scenario of exact knowledge of a target value, yielding consequences for inertial gradient flows applied to minimization problems with constraints. Additionally, these methods are adaptable to include noise, thereby facilitating applications within the field of inverse problems.

This study examines the phase transitions in algorithms designed for robots to navigate walls, specifically examining how varying levels of noise impact the macroscopic behavior of individual micro-mechanisms. The researchers derived an analytical model for a deterministic, multi-cell automaton and utilized it to characterize transition phases across diverse robotic configurations. The findings indicate that the macroscopic behavior of this specific multi-cell system is directly governed by the phase transitions within its constituent deterministic cells. Furthermore, a comparison was made between this deterministic system and a stochastic variant, which incorporates noise into the cellular reduction process. The analysis of the resulting phase diagrams highlights key distinctions and similarities between the two approaches, with the thermodynamic limit of the deterministic system serving as a foundational reference for interpreting the behavior of the stochastic robot algorithm.

A self-consistent approach to the disordered Anderson model, incorporating a simplified kinetic-energy-driven non-Fermi liquid spectrum, is used to investigate the normal state properties of cuprates. By solving the resulting nonperturbative and energy-dependent impurity self-energy via a renormalization group method, we examine how a finite concentration of extended impurities influences transport. The study reveals that for sufficiently large extension, the system undergoes a metal-insulator transition at a specific critical concentration. Additionally, the conductivity's characteristic energy scale, or crossover frequency, displays a doping-dependent shift to the microwave regime and an implicit dependence on the impurity's energy profile, both of which align with and help explain experimental observations.

This work examines a model of curvature evolution, defined as $u_{\tau}\tau = H_{\varepsilon} + \alpha_{t}\delta_{t}$, which exhibits crystalline characteristics akin to the evolution of mean curvature. In survey form, this research elucidates the model's fundamental properties, including its connection to viscosity solutions of associated curvature equations, curvature-dependent variational models, and geometric curvature equations. Additionally, this analysis bridges these diverse formulations and highlights their interconnections, while curating an extensive collection of open questions for future inquiry.

Plants are essential for our daily lives, yet growing them can be challenging for those lacking gardening knowledge. To address this, we introduce GrowSpace, a virtual simulation designed to help users cultivate various plants by making decisions regarding care and monitoring based on a visible health meter. Its user interface allows selecting plant species and adjusting water, light, and temperature settings. We developed a policy for managing a plant's health by analyzing interaction data from 100 random trials across 200 instances for each of 13 plant species. To achieve precise control over plant growth, we developed two reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO and DQN, to optimize the care strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that our learned policies effectively replicate real-world gardening dynamics, accurately modeling how different species respond to varying environmental conditions.

The Schramm-Loewner evolution with parameter $\kappa=4$ (SLE$_4$) emerges as the statistical mechanics of loops within two-dimensional (2) quantum gravity. This finding establishes a tangible relationship between 2D quantum gravity and the conformal geometry of SLE$_4$, akin to how Brownian motion relates to the conformal structure of a unit disk. The analysis further utilizes techniques from non-commutative probability theory to explicitly formulate the conformal welding of quantum disks.

This review outlines the functions and achievements of the IBNI, an open consortium dedicated to advancing radiomic reproducibility. We examine the scientific rationale and progress made in preclinical and clinical radiomics, while addressing the substantial reproducibility challenges identified. The paper details the progress of the IBNI in developing solutions to counter these radiomic reproducibility issues, with a specific focus on nomenclature, data sharing, and normalization.
