Software debugging is a critical software engineering activity that frequently requires locating the parts of a codebase affected by a bug. While existing code comprehension tools typically rely on developer-provided information, such as comments, to function, this data is often scarce or insufficient. Although Natural Language Processing (NLP) could potentially address this gap, it faces a significant hurdle: developers tend to describe problems using domain-specific jargon that differs from standard natural language. To bridge this linguistic divide, we introduce QUICKAR, a novel framework that automatically generates multiple informal inquiries about a code segment. These varied formulations are then leveraged to enhance existing code searching capabilities. Our approach employs a transformer-based architecture to create both general and domain-aligned variations for a single input question. By utilizing crowd-sourced technical information, QUICKAR automatically derives domain-aligned terms and phrases to create tailored question variations. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy substantially surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy for code visualization tasks.

Entraining represents a fundamental mechanism in conversational interaction, where individuals subtly synchronize their acoustic behaviors to create an acoustic bond, thereby signaling social closeness. Previous investigations have primarily examined this phenomenon through controlled, lab-based experiments utilizing specific acoustic metrics. This study introduces a methodology to assess entrainment by applying deep learning techniques to automatically identify regions of shared acoustic behaviors. The proposed approach involves training a recurrent neural network on extensive, spontaneous speech datasets to model acoustic dependencies and measuring the predicted deviations from these models for utterances as indicators of entrainment levels. Utilizing the Switchboard corpus, the research demonstrates that acoustic entrainment correlates with participants' geographical proximity and mutual liking. The analysis further reveals a dynamic evolution of these effects across conversation turns, reflecting the progressive nature of entrainment.

Imaging data, particularly when combined with spectral information, is becoming increasingly common in biological and medical research. To address this, the authors developed RCSEDv2, an enhanced version of the open-source ImageJ/FIJI plugins introduced in 2019 as the RCSEDi plugin. This updated plugin offers three key features: a Graphical User Interface (GUI) for generating and viewing rCIF and CIF file formats, the ImageJ Server API for multi-core processing capabilities, and a Microscope GUI extension to facilitate direct integration with live microscopy systems.

This research addresses the challenge of Temporal Action Segmentation (TAS) in unlabelled settings. While numerous unsupervised approaches have been developed, they typically depend on pre-trained models trained on extensive labeled datasets, which restricts their applicability to scenarios where such models are also unavailable. In this work, we introduce an unsupervised TAS framework that eliminates the need for any external pretrained dependencies. By leveraging two core principles—enhancing action representation and capturing temporal characteristics—we propose Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Analysis (SSCA). This framework utilizes a self-supervised strategy to analyze video pairs featuring different fixed temporal bounds, generating support cues that enable accurate action segmentation. Extensive evaluations on the Kinetics-400 dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 21.8%, surpassing current state-of-the-art unsupervised methods. Additionally, the code for this implementation can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/zhenghao-zhuang/SSCA}.

The article investigates the production, decay, and coupling of concealed-charm pentaquark states. Employed current algebra methods enable the derivation of these quantitative parameters directly from $B$-meson semi-exclusive decays into charm-light meson-pairs, specifically targeting $B \to PP$ processes that generate $B \to c\bar{c} + (c\bar{q}, q\bar{q}')$ transitions. The calculated couplings and branching ratios for $B$-decays provide a means to determine the production cross-sections of such pentaquarks in high-energy proton-proton ($pp$) collisions. The study finds that pentaquark states possessing internal charm loops are predominantly produced via the $t$-channel mechanism, whereas those without charm loops arise mainly from $u$-channel processes. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that $B$-physics findings offer a distinct advantage over purely kinematical approaches, which previously relied on unmeasured relative production cross-sections in $pp$ environments.

In software testing, there is a growing need to develop stronger analytical skills among students and professionals. To meet this demand, we developed a tool that evaluates student testing responses and offers targeted feedback. Our approach analyzes test automation syntax to pinpoint specific defects in students' testing strategies, then delivers inquiry-based feedback that encourages critical thinking and further investigation. We empirically compared this system against a traditional, detailed feedback mechanism to determine its efficacy. Our findings indicate that inquiry-based, conceptual feedback outperforms thorough, detailed feedback in enhancing software testing abilities. Additionally, students receiving inquiry-based feedback demonstrated significantly higher engagement levels. These results suggest that targeted feedback can effectively improve testing competencies while maintaining high learner engagement.

Domain adaptation is essential for deploying machine learning models in real-world scenarios where data collection is costly and subject to distribution shifts. While source-target pair-wise adaptation methods exist, source-free settings are gaining prominence as source data becomes inaccessible. This paper introduces a semi-supervised hypothesis shift framework designed to adapt to target domains using only labeled target samples and clean samples obtained by filtering noisy data through a semi-supervised process. The method employs two complementary mechanisms: first, a semi-supervised process that identifies clean samples by leveraging mutual consistency and low entropy to mitigate label noise and improve data quality; second, a multi-objective optimization strategy that aligns distributions, maximizes mutual manifold alignment, and ensures the separation of class clusters. Empirical evaluations across three standard target shift benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over current state-of-the-art solutions.

The paper proposes a gas-core nuclear thermal rocket capable of reaching specific impulses exceeding 500 seconds, designed for space missions requiring high propulsion efficiency. This core concept leverages direct rocket thrust from internal combustion gases, distinguishing it from traditional designs.

We introduce a domain-informed neural network designed to determine the location of interactions in particle detectors. This framework demonstrates the potential of integrating prior physical domain knowledge into neural architectures to enhance model interpretability and reduce data requirements for training. Specifically, we leverage two key features astroparticle detectors: their bounded volume and their capacity to isolate interactions occurring within a defined central region. First, we employ a convolutional neural network to transform interactions into Cartesian coordinates relative to the target central area. Second, we convert the detector geometry into a point cloud to align precisely with the region of interest. These adaptations significantly decrease the model dependence on extensive training data and improve its generalizability. Using realistic simulations from the RENO experiment, we confirm that this approach yields accurate and essentially equivalent results to those of models trained directly in energy and time domains.

Atmospheric characterization of exoplanets and stellar atmospheres depends on determining the physical properties of absorbing molecules. This process involves comparing observed spectra with synthetic models, where the models are generated by convolving the physics of molecular absorption with a line-by-line database using absorption cross-sections. While such a line-by-line approach is currently standard for stars and stellar-mass objects, it remains unfeasible for low-mass brown dwarfs and orbiting giant exoplanets due to the extreme computational demands of integrating realistic spectra from dense cross-section data. To resolve this, we introduce EXOPLINES, a dedicated database of pre-computed molecular absorption cross-sections tailored specifically for simulating the atmospheres of these low-mass objects.

We introduce the concept of the "ground" ground within answer set programming, formalizing it as a first-order extension of predicate logic first developed by Delgrande et al. (2001). In this framework, the semantic link between a ground and its associated answer sets is mediated by logical implication. We examine various forms of ground through the lens of their syntactical and semantic components, utilizing both classical and non-classical logics. The discussion highlights the interplay between grounds and normal, as well as ground and semi-grounded programs. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these structures and the broader class of non-monotonic logical theories.

We introduce an initial law governing quantum resource theories, which serves as a broad generalization of thermodynamics. This framework addresses resource conversion between states within the same theory, constrained solely by the specific nature of those conversions. By defining key quantities to quantify state transformation costs, we establish initial laws that formalize resource conservation. These laws are derived exclusively from postulates inherent to axiomatic thermodynamics and remain valid regardless of whether the states involved are quantum or classical. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of this approach by deriving existing results in thermodynamics, asymmetry, and entanglement theory as direct implications of initial laws.

We introduce a new method for modeling datasets with unknown parameters using a moment function that needs to be identified first. A data-generating process is proposed where a specific moment function's population-level moment is set to a known value. The proposed estimation method involves finding an empirical non-negative measure on the support space that satisfies this moment condition. The method is shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal, with a finite sample demonstration using a simple Poisson model. The simulation results suggest that the method is robust to misspecification of the moment function, with asymptotic optimality in a specific sense. This study examines heavy-tailed, multivariate time series influenced by exogenous shocks, utilizing a recent framework established by the authors that accommodates time-varying dependencies and shifts in dimensionality. We present a novel approach for modeling and forecasting such series, introducing flexible methods for forecasting future shocks and their marginal distributions. We establish that the proposed methods are robust against violations of the assumed shock distribution shapes and demonstrate their effectiveness through simulations and by analyzing real-world financial data.

Quantum error correction is vital for error mitigation in quantum computing, yet most existing decoders for these errors are either inefficient or fail to guarantee rapid convergence. This study introduces a speed-enhanced decoder capable of operating linearly in time relative to the code's size. This approach targets a specific category of good low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that include those derived from high girth expander graphs and high girth random ensembles. We demonstrate that this decoder achieves error correction with a probability approaching one, provided the error rate remains below a constant threshold. Furthermore, its time complexity scales linearly with both the block length and the number of correction steps required, regardless of the circuit depth. We also present a variant of this decoder capable of pinpointing the location of errors with a high degree of certainty.

This study investigates how disorder affects second-order topological insulators (2DOTIs) within a tight-binding framework. We demonstrate that the correlation length of edge and corner zero-energy states remains constant despite increasing impurity strength, a finding that contrasts sharply with conventional topological and trivial insulators, where localization length diminishes under similar conditions. This observation supports the existence of a "bulk-surface correspondence" in 2DOTIs, which extends the well-established "bulk-boundary correspondence." Additionally, our findings align with recent theoretical work predicting disorder resilience in 2DOTIs, further confirming the stability of higher-order topological states when surface correlation scales remain disordered-independent.

We present a straightforward approach for real-time rendering of novel views from a set of photographs. The method integrates a differentiable forward model of coherent light transport with optimized per-image parameters of a compact deep network. This framework enables the synthesis of new views by jointly optimizing both the environment and object representations.

In 2021, the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile conducted a series of speckle interferometry observations. This study targeted 15 young stellar objects (YSOs) located within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and the Tarantula Nebula (N343), a region approximately 165,000 light-years distant. The primary objective was to resolve potential circumstellar disks and rings by examining these YSOs. Data were gathered using the 4.1-meter Wide Field Optical Camera and Spectrograph (WFISS) in the $I_C$ filter, which has a diffraction limit of roughly 0.37 arcseconds. The image reconstruction process utilized the SPECKLE software package. The analysis revealed that four YSOs exhibited clear binary systems, while another four showed probable binary configurations. Furthermore, one YSO displayed a distinct circumstellar ring or disk structure. These findings are consistent with previous research and suggest that future observations with next-generation 30-meter class telescopes will yield even more detailed results.

Magnetic reconnection in the solar corona is a primary mechanism for energy release, often triggering mass ejections that propagate through the complex magnetic environment. While the phenomena associated with these events are well-documented, the specific dynamics of how a leading piston pushes surrounding plasma remain unclear. This study presents new findings on a coronal mass flow driven by reconnection near active region 12673 during the solar minimum. We detected a shock wave moving supersonically through dense, cool plasma at approximately 10,000 K, a scenario rarely observed. Utilizing extensive radio observations from the LOFAR array, we tracked the shock wave and the resulting radio emission as it traversed the cool plasma. Our analysis indicates that the shock expands into a spherical structure with a radius of roughly 100,000 km, behaving similarly to a jet-driven piston blast. This specific event offers a rare opportunity to examine piston-driven shocks within the cool, low-coronal regions.

The two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) remains a prominent framework for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model, offering a natural solution to stabilizing the Higgs mass while accommodating a rich phenomenology. This study performs a likelihood-based analysis of flavour anomalies and the experimental deviation in the muon anomalous magnetic moment ($g-2$) within a generalized 2HDM. By employing the four-parameter basis, we assess the model's viability. Our results indicate that a light charged Higgs, with a mass below 500 GeV, can effectively address the flavour anomalies. However, the same parameter space required to explain the $g-2$ anomaly is mutually exclusive with the one fitting these flavour anomalies. Consequently, the model cannot simultaneously explain both sets of observations.

We present a novel, exact stochastic differential equation describing the time evolution of vortex filaments in a 3D incompressible fluid subjected to external forcing and noise. Extending the standard Navier-Stokes equations, our modified system incorporates the back-reaction caused by statistical effects, which significantly alters trajectory correlations and diffusion patterns of individual vortices. Notably, even with the presence of a small total noise composed of a Navier-Stokes viscous term, this correction produces substantial changes in vortex dynamics. Additionally, because our enhanced framework remains valid near equilibrium, it offers a robust extension of the Overlap Model applicable in three dimensions.

Boson sampling serves as a theoretical framework designed to showcase quantum supremacy by sampling the output probabilities of indistinguishable photons passing through a random linear optical circuit; however, prior research has largely examined this process solely through the lens of quantum walk theory. This study proposes a novel perspective by utilizing the full quantum state sampling complete state, which allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the global entanglement characteristics within boson sampling. We demonstrate that the global entanglement present in this state exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with the number of inputs, implying that neither few-nor highly populated systems are optimal for achieving quantum advantage. Furthermore, we reveal that while quantum entanglement scales polynomially with both the sample inputs and circuit components within the global state, this relationship becomes super-polynomial when focusing exclusively on sub-nuclear states. We also observe a non-trivial correlation between global and partial entanglement in these states, noting that controlling the former enables the prediction of the latter. These findings offer valuable insights for future investigations into quantum advantage and the evolution of entanglement.

We introduce a novel supervised algorithm for the high-precision prediction of high-dimensional sequences, specifically those with short temporal lengths, addressing the specific demands of time-series life science data. In contrast to standard deep learning architectures, our approach utilizes a guidance mechanism to efficiently extract features from input time-series. Using measurements of mouse brain activity, we successfully classified neural states, achieving high classification accuracy with a computational cost that remains constant regardless of dimension count.

This paper investigates the utility of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) within partially observable settings. We demonstrate that RNNs function as internal buffers for past observations, enabling agents to act effectively despite limited environmental visibility. Our analysis reveals that in such domains, RNN-enhanced policies form a specific class of belief-to-action (B2A) mappings. These policies operate by integrating the network's output with observation histories to construct a sufficient history (SH)—a condensed summary containing all data essential for optimality. We illustrate this mechanism through a simplified grid-world scenario, showing how an RNN learns to store past observations as internal states, effectively using these to build the necessary SH for efficient operation.

To further validate these findings, we examined a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) inspired by the "Hidden Word Task," which requires building the SH from sequential inputs. In this context, RNNs successfully emulate the ideal B2A mapping, utilizing their internal states to represent the required SH. We also explored a more complex variation involving variable-length inputs and multiple possible histories of optimal length. Here, RNNs approximate the optimal strategy by using a limited capacity to retain only the most relevant history components for optimal action selection.

Human Action Detection (HAD) is a significant yet difficult challenge in computer vision, typically formulated as a per-frame, per-pixel classification task. However, pixel-level annotations are costly and hard to acquire, leading to the prevalence of weak supervision, where object class labels are provided only for entire video sequences rather than frame by frame. This paper introduces the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to the domain of weakly supervised HAD. By modeling video data as an adjacency matrix, the proposed method facilitates the aggregation of contextual information across time and space. Additionally, the approach is extended to operate on partially labeled data. Experiments conducted on the Charades-ANN dataset demonstrate that this strategy yields state-of-the-art performance in weakly supervised HAD.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC) aimed to evaluate and compare various methods for determining whether pairs of images originate from the same visual concept. This challenge was organized as a binary classification task, requiring models to determine if two images share a category. It included a comprehensive dataset of 60,000 labeled pairs representing 102 distinct classes. Participants were able to submit predictions for all test pair combinations or utilize a subset of these via a specific data partitioning strategy. The evaluation framework employed a combination of the F1 score and an adapted version of normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) to rank submissions. This study details the challenge's organization, dataset characteristics, and assessment methodologies, while also analyzing participant outcomes and identifying the top-performing approaches.

The work is driven by the need to address three specific challenges: the boundary issue in Schrödinger's equation with a linear potential; the issue of metastability associated with multiscale nonlinear Schrödinger's equation; and the problem of domain homogenization in the parabolic framework. The study begins with the analysis of the underlying diffusion and perturbed processes, with the analysis of the boundary issue depending on the precise asymptotics of the associated functional for the perturbed process. The analysis of the homogenization problem is based on the asymptotics of the expected value of the first exit time for the perturbed process, while the investigation of the problem of metastability is based on the analysis of the first exit time for the perturbed process on the boundary of the domain. This study explores the impact of intense magnetic fields on the properties of nuclear matter. Utilizing the Local Density Approximation, we applied the Local Density Operator technique to derive the nuclear equation of state and other essential parameters, such as the speed of sound and incompressibility. Our results demonstrate that a strong external magnetic field significantly alters the equation of state, incompressibility, and speed of sound, leading to a marked reduction in incompressibility. These findings are expected to benefit researchers investigating the behavior of neutron stars and magnetars.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a privacy-preserving distributed machine learning framework that avoids sharing raw data by training across client devices. However, current privacy-preserving FL approaches often incur high computational and communication costs, rendering them impractical for resource-constrained environments. This work introduces DP-REC, the initial methodology to integrate Differential Privacy (DP) and Secure Remote Execution (SRE) for FL, thereby delivering a solution that is both privacy-tough and communication-efficient. By adopting a server-centric model, these techniques eliminate the need for clients to embed complex and costly deep learning frameworks, thereby significantly lowering communication overhead. The authors also present a novel, communication-efficient all-reduce algorithm that cuts communication costs by up to 75% compared to standard protocols. Empirical evaluations on standard image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve substantial gains in both communication efficiency and privacy protection.

The Far-UV Explorer (FLEX) mission, a proposed far-ultraviolet space observatory, is designed to investigate the interstellar medium (ISM) within the Taurus, Perseus, and Aquila star-forming regions. By utilizing FLEX's 11-channel imaging spectrometer, researchers can analyze the spatial distribution of far-ultraviolet (FUV) emission and its spectral characteristics to determine the physical and chemical makeup of the interstellar gas and dust. The study focuses on identifying FUV emission sources, including diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs), molecular emissions, and point-source contributions. These sources are analyzed in the context of the region's massive stars, stellar winds, and the general far-UV background. The analysis reveals that the majority of FUV emission originates from diffuse interstellar clouds, with a notable correlation between emission intensity and hydrogen column density. Additionally, emission from dense molecular clouds is detected, with intensity scaling with molecular mass. The research also highlights significant point-source emissions from Herbig Be stars, which exhibit strong molecular FUV signals. Furthermore, spectral analysis of the emission reveals that the far-UV background in these regions is dominated by molecular emissions, with a distinct spectral signature dominated by the molecular band at 1216 Å.

Tables are frequently used to present data in research papers, reports, and documentation. Manual searching for these tables is inefficient, leading to a significant waste of time. This study introduces a solution to locate relevant tables within PDF documents using natural language queries. We suggest an approach that leverages graph neural networks to create table representations. Initially, table cells are transformed into a directed graph using relationships, and node embeddings are generated via graph convolutional networks. These serve as the foundation for table representation learning. We also introduce a table representation learning method based on the Table2Text task, where Table2Text involves generating text descriptions from tables. Experiments show that our approach outperforms existing methods by 10% in the Table2Context task and achieves a 20% improvement over the current state-of-the-art models.

This paper investigates a multi-stage game involving sequential players, a specific type known as a "cognitive game," which models conflicts where participants have varying levels of access to information regarding their opponents' capabilities. The core contribution is the introduction of a "hierarchy of cognition," a recursive framework describing how players anticipate their opponents' potential moves and the reasoning behind them. We demonstrate the existence of "hierarchy-equivalent" equilibria, proving that multiple rounds of such thinking yield an increasing number of essential outcomes. The analysis also covers the implications for equilibria when the hierarchy count is limited or undefined, establishing that the limit of these cognitive levels does not alter the equilibrium set if all players share the same depth of thought. Furthermore, we prove that if one player possesses strictly superior hierarchical reasoning compared to their rivals, they are guaranteed to secure a superior payoff.

This study examines the application of deep learning for the continuous, waste-free estimation of population counts using autonomous vehicle data in Mozambique. By integrating data from the 2017 and 2021 census rounds, we train a model to estimate population density across a 200-meter grid for each scene. Our analysis reveals that our method achieves 76.2% accuracy in this task. Furthermore, we utilize this technique to validate the accuracy of the 2021 census and project future population growth, demonstrating that the approach can be integrated into the census framework to supply reliable population estimates on a regular schedule.

The approximate membership query (AMQ) problem involves efficiently and compactly determining whether elements belong to a dynamic collection of items, allowing for a bounded probability of error. This study introduces the first AMQ algorithm that completely eliminates false negatives while maintaining a constant-number of bits. In contrast, prior methods typically sacrifice either sensitivity accuracy or space efficiency. Furthermore, we present the first sublinear-time Bloom filter variant capable of withstanding a constant fraction of deletions while preserving a fixed, constant rate of false positives. We also provide implementations of AMQ for two additional data structures: the skip list and the hash tree, each utilizing only a constant number of bits per element.

This study explores how to create spinor molecules from spinor atoms through three-body recombination driven by an adiabatically varied laser. We demonstrate that this process is governed by a specific effective Hamiltonian featuring linear and bilinear couplings between molecular and atomic states. By analyzing the corresponding Bloch equations, we identify the conditions necessary to maximize conversion efficiency from atoms to molecules. Furthermore, we outline a strategy to selectively prepare specific spin states of the resulting spinor molecules.

Validated against a moving mesh method, our method demonstrates that resolution requirements for fluid flow can be lower than those for fluid-structure interaction problems, with accurate results confirmed against a mesh method, showing good agreement in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The field of quantum machine learning is rapidly expanding, with recent strides in algorithms and hardware making it a compelling area for research. This work introduces a quantum version of the well-established k-means unsupervised algorithm, which is being adapted for integration into larger quantum-aided machine learning frameworks. We detail the implementation of this model on both a simulation environment and IBM's 5-qubit superconducting processor key findings include performance matching that of classical k-means on simulation data and the successful execution of the algorithm on a real quantum device for the first time, marking a significant step in applying machine learning models to high-dimensional datasets using actual quantum hardware.

Pitch is a fundamental element of human speech, and recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS) technology have enabled its dynamic manipulation. Among the leading synthetic speech generation models, FastPitch is renowned for its high-quality output and efficient inference. However, it suffers from pitch controllability issues, often producing unnatural pitch contours that result in poor speech quality. To address this, the proposed approach enhances FastPitch's pitch controllability by integrating an unsupervised learning-based pitch augmentation algorithm. This method increases the density of input pitch targets around their mean values while utilizing a time-frequency domain-based, timbre-preserving warping strategy to ensure speech characteristics remain intact. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique yields significant enhancements in both pitch controllability metrics and overall speech quality.

This paper introduces Hopper, a new multilevel prediction method designed for complex spatiotemporal tasks. Unlike previous approaches that often fail to handle multi-step forecasting, Hopper effectively addresses scenarios requiring multiple predictions. Its architecture integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with a hierarchical structure to enhance both accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, it employs a dynamic feature extraction module that adapts to varying prediction horizons, while a novel feature fusion layer combines information from multiple temporal levels to refine final outputs. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that Hopper surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in performance, achieving significant improvements in both prediction precision and inference speed.

This study introduces a novel method for determining the mass of the $W$ boson, utilizing a $ll^{\prime}\bar{b}b^{\prime}$ event topology where the electron and muon are identified in the leptonic decays of the $W$ and Higgs bosons. The analysis employs full matrix element weighting to simultaneously account for the differential cross section and the experimental detector resolution. The measurement utilizes 13.6~TeV collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 13.9~fb$^{-1}$. The $W$ boson mass is determined to be $m_{W} = 80\,400 \pm 130 \,\text{(stat)} \pm 110 \,\text{(syst)}$~MeV. This result is consistent with previous LHC measurements and aligns with Standard Model predictions.

Telepresence robots hold promise for remote participation in social events and professional settings, yet current systems lack effective remote presence quality of experience (QoE) models. This research introduces a new framework for designing telepresence robot control systems by modeling the user experience through a lens of remote presence QoE. The framework centers on a "remoteness" metric that quantifies the user's capacity to engage in social interaction and professional duties via a screen. It establishes a functional relationship between system design parameters and remoteness, utilizing this basis to develop an interactive design space. The method involves generating design space curves via interactive curve selection, which allows users to balance competing QoE factors and specify ideal system configurations. The space serves both as a mechanism for defining optimal settings and a research tool for analyzing the QoE landscape of remote systems. Validation through a study with 100 participants indicates that this approach is effective for creating and characterizing the QoE of telepresence technology.

This brief guide offers a smooth entry into Bayesian hierarchical linear analysis. It explores key model components, how to specify them, and analyze and interpret the results. The discussion is supported by examples from both categorical and continuous outcome data, with all demonstrations based on widely used public datasets accessible via the `bayesflex` R package.

This paper establishes a precise mathematical framework for the Mafia game, an asynchronous social deduction model, by defining it through a structured set of game states and valid moves. The analysis rigorously examines the core mechanics, particularly the critical role of public discussion and announcement phases in shaping the game's dynamics. The core objective is to identify specific attributes of the initial configuration that determine the ultimate victory for either the Mafia or the Good guys. Ultimately, the authors present a novel approach to proving victory for the Mafia by utilizing a unique graph, offering distinct insights into the game's underlying structure.

This study investigates a scenario where two giant planets form within a restricted mass range close to the core-accretion threshold, remaining planet-like until gas accretion commences. We analyze how mutual gas accretion influences their ultimate masses and examine the dynamical feedback between the evolving planetary system and the protoplanetary disk. Using a code that integrates planet formation and disk evolution, we simulate this interaction, revealing that planet-planet interactions can significantly alter planet masses and disk architecture. Specifically, near a critical disk mass, a temporary decoupling of planet growth and disk evolution can occur, allowing one planet to rapidly increase in mass while the other stagnates. This dynamic can persist for up to approximately 100,000 years, resulting in a mass disparity of a factor up to 3.5. Furthermore, these planet-planet interactions can reconfigure the gap in a gaseous disk, shifting its location by up to 20 astronomical units. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for dynamical processes when modeling the formation of giant planets and their subsequent evolution.

Electron transport within a film of single-walled carbon nanotubes is primarily attributed to intertube hopping, a process that has been theorized to be governed by phonon-assisted tunneling. This study provides the first experimental validation of this mechanism through temperature-dependent measurements of macroscopic film conductivity. The data aligns with a tight-binding model that incorporates both phonon-assisted tunneling and variable contact resistance, which is itself temperature-dependent. Furthermore, the research demonstrates a correlation between these contact parameters and the degree of tube entanglement, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy.

Fuzzy clustering is a popular technique for partitioning unlabeled datasets by assigning samples to multiple clusters based on their similarity, a method particularly effective for identifying overlapping patterns. However, traditional approaches like the fuzzy *k*-means algorithm face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional data, primarily due to the curse of dimensionality, which distorts distance metrics and reduces accuracy. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel fuzzy *k*-means variant designed specifically for high-dimensional environments. This new algorithm employs a weighted feature mechanism where the influence of each dimension on sample-cluster distance is adjusted according to the feature's own distance from the cluster center. Furthermore, the weights associated with features for any given sample are determined dynamically based on the sample's entropy relative to different clusters. Experimental results across both low and high-dimensional datasets confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing algorithms in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has become a cornerstone in deep learning, driving significant advancements in natural language processing and vision tasks. This work establishes a rigorous statistical learning theory for MoE, investigating high-dimensional regression with $p$ features and $K$ expert components. We analyze both sparse models, where only $s$ out of $K$ experts are activated per prediction, and dense models, where all experts contribute. We introduce the first algorithms that consistently achieve high-dimensional statistical minimax lower bounds across both configurations. For the sparse case specifically, we provide a complete characterization of the statistical risk in terms of key parameters including $p$, $K$, $s$, and the sample size $n$. These findings directly address and resolve prior negative results from the literature. Additionally, we present a novel, computationally efficient algorithm with linear computational complexity that surpasses existing methods in both performance and speed.

Refraction, a phenomenon typically associated with classical optics, has been recently proposed as a diagnostic for quantum gravity effects, specifically the disruption of global symmetries leading to modified dispersion relations. By investigating the double refraction of a high-energy photon traversing a quantum gravitational medium, researchers can test quantum gravity models. In this study, we analyze constraints on such models derived from the absence of double refraction during the 2019 detection of a high-energy gamma-ray burst (GRB 190114C) by the Fermi-LAT instrument. We further assess these constraints in relation to recent findings regarding black hole complementarity.

We utilized data from the UVIT telescope aboard the AstroSat satellite to analyze 40 UV bright stars in the globular cluster NGC 4147, which are significantly more luminous than the cluster's main sequence turnoff (MSTO). These stars were identified in the UV band specifically, though they are notably absent from optical surveys due to this detection bias. Our findings indicate that these stars are primarily located on the blue horizontal branch (BHB), with a secondary population on the red horizontal branch (HRF). The study reveals that these stars possess surface gravities and temperatures comparable to those of BHB stars in other globular clusters. Furthermore, their effective temperatures are higher than those of BHB stars in the cluster's red giant branch (RHF) counterparts. These observations suggest that the thermal properties of these stars are a result of their evolutionary state, rather than any unique internal mechanism. We conclude that these stars are a unique class of objects that have not been previously identified in the literature.

Transfer learning is widely employed to address the two- Agreement challenge in deep learning: leveraging knowledge from a source task to enhance performance on a target task when labeled data is scarce. While prior research has predominantly focused on enhancing feature or task alignment, this study argues that ensuring the Transferability of Task-Feature Consistency (TFC) is the critical factor for successful knowledge transfer. We first identify three fundamental properties of effective Transferability—high similarity between tasks, high compatibility between tasks, and high consistency between tasks—and demonstrate through a theoretical framework that TFC is the most essential property. We then introduce a novel, unsupervised method to learn a unified representation space that explicitly optimizes for all three properties. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving severe label data limitations.

The rapid spread of information across social media platforms significantly impacts the economics of online content. This study investigates how the topological structure of social networks influences the 2-D diffusion of information, specifically examining how network modularity shapes information propagation dynamics. We propose a novel model featuring a single source and heterogeneous agents operating within multiple communities of varying sizes, where inter-community links are established via a preferential attachment mechanism. We analyze the temporal evolution of cumulative adopters and identify a specific modularity threshold that maximizes information diffusion speed. Furthermore, we determine an optimal value for this modularity threshold that minimizes the total adoption cost. These findings underscore the critical role of network structure in shaping information diffusion processes, thereby offering valuable insights for social networking platforms and online content creators.

Thomas-Yau's 1-folding conjecture posits that the topological type distinctiveness of a hypersurface within a compact Riemannian manifold is the sole determinant of its index in the sorted index set of all such hypersurfaces. This conjecture was previously divided into qualitative and quantitative forms; the current study addresses the latter. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any given compact, convex hypersurface exhibiting zero total mean curvature, the index gap relative to the maximal possible index is bounded from below by a function of its total curvature and the volume of the ambient space. This paper also examines the scope and boundaries of the quantitative problem.

Software vulnerabilities are a primary driver of evasion attacks, which are increasingly common and pose a severe threat to modern systems. Among mobile platforms, Android stands as the most widely adopted, hosting mobile applications that handle highly sensitive data. To mitigate these risks, Android has rolled out Issue-Space Evasion (ISE) attacks designed to bypass malicious code by exploiting the OS's inherent flaws. This survey provides an in-depth examination of ISE attacks within the Android ecosystem, covering their foundational principles, a detailed breakdown of specific cases, and the underlying strategies of the attack. Furthermore, the paper explores potential countermeasures to defend against such threats and identifies key avenues for future research.

While numerous general-purpose container orchestration systems exist, few are suited for diverse workloads. This paper introduces Ozy, a universal orchestration framework capable of managing heterogeneous tasks ranging from simple processes and batch jobs to microservices, batch processing, and containerized applications. By unifying these capabilities, Ozy delivers streamlined operations and enhanced efficiency. The research details the system's design and implementation, supported by a comprehensive set of experiments. The results demonstrate that Ozy effectively manages a wide spectrum of tasks while achieving superior performance and resource utilization compared to existing solutions.

The ground state of fractional quantum Hall systems with 5 or more electrons is typically predicted to be the Laughlin state carrying fractional charge. However, recent findings indicate that under moderate Landau level mixing, the ground state can shift to a distinct topological phase. This new phase is characterized by a different Chern number, fractional charge, and edge states, and is often referred to as the reentrant phase. In this study, we examine the ground state of a 5-elector system subjected to strong Land level mixing. Our findings reveal that although the system remains in the Chern number = 1 phase, it does not transition to the anticipated reentrant phase. This result suggests that the reentrant phase may only manifest under extremely strong mixing conditions, or that the transition is more complex than previously thought.

Although the theoretical possibility of black holes existing in the early universe is well-established, the lack of observational evidence has led to the conclusion that their density is negligible. In this work, however, we demonstrate a novel solution to the Einstein equations, which describes black holes in the presence of a perfect fluid. This metric aligns with the Thakurta metric when the fluid behaves as dust. By examining the characteristics of this Thakurta-like solution, we identify a significant discrepancy: the two metrics differ in their asymptotic behavior. This difference implies that the Thakurta metric does not accurately represent black holes within the fluid context. We further demonstrate that the Thakurta metric fails to describe black holes in the dust-dominated early universe, whereas the solution derived in the current work does accurately capture their properties. Additionally, we assess the constraints on the abundance of primordial black holes (PBHs) during the dust-dominated epoch. Our findings indicate that these constraints remain unaffected by the theoretical distinctions highlighted in this study.

Planet formation via pebble accretion is a critical phase in protoplanetary disc evolution, yet the impact of density fluctuations on this process remains uncertain. This study investigates how such fluctuations influence the growth rate of protoplanets. We conducted a series of 2D hydrodynamic simulations to generate density maps representing various fluctuation amplitudes and spatial scales. By averaging over these realizations, we assessed the influence of these variations on time-averaged accretion rates. Our results indicate that the mean accretion rate is modulated by density variations across a range of scales. Specifically, the enhancement in accretion due to fluctuations can reach up to 20% when the amplitude varies by a factor of 2 and the spatial scale factor ($f$) falls between 0.1 and 0.4 relative to the protoplanet's Hill radius. Consequently, the "mass gap" observed between super-Earths and sub-neptunes may be mitigated through pebble accretion within inhomogeneous environments.

The overparameterization of neural networks has been linked to their success, prompting the hypothesis that restricting the optimization process to computationally feasible methods necessitates a higher number of parameters to perform effectively. We demonstrate this connection by showing that within a computationally restricted framework, only a specific subset of parameters can be efficiently trained using a backpropagation-based stochastic gradient descent. We then establish performance lower bounds for networks with constrained optimization, covering various tasks and architectures. Finally, we empirically confirm these findings and extend them to deeper networks, supporting the proposed computational theory of overparameterization.

This work addresses the distribution of Bohr sets within sumsets in the context of countable abelian groups, continuing the analysis initiated in [1]. We demonstrate that within the $n$-fold sum of a finite, non-empty subset $A$ in any such group, the minimal size of a Bohr set where $A$ is relatively uniformly distributed is bounded by $O(\log |A|/\log(N))$, where $N$ denotes the countable cardinality of the ambient group. Furthermore, we establish that this bound is optimal up to a multiplicative constant. The primary techniques employed are combinatorial methods, specifically leveraging Freiman-type rank and structure theorems, alongside additive tools, including Ruzsa's "smoothing" approach.

This paper introduces a new optimization problem known as the Urban Dial-a-Ride (UDAR). In this context, a fleet of vehicles must collect customers at specific pick-up points along fixed urban routes to execute door-to-door transport. The objective is to determine the number of vehicles required and their respective routes while minimizing total cost and strictly adhering to time windows at both pick-up and drop-off locations. Since UDAR represents an NP-hard challenge, we developed a solution approach based on Branch-and-Cut. This method utilizes a polyhedral study to formulate an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) model, which is subsequently strengthened by deriving valid inequalities. Among these, we define two novel classes of constraints tailored to UDAR specifics and establish the corresponding polytope's key properties. Finally, we outline a branch-and-cuts algorithm incorporating these constraints, demonstrating its efficacy through computational results that prove its effectiveness.

Multi-Pretraining (MUP) has become a standard technique for addressing various e-commerce challenges, yet its current implementation relies solely on input modality sequences, failing to effectively capture the deep semantic connections between eText and eImage data. To address this limitation, we introduce KUMP, a KNowledge-Understood Multi-modal Pretraining framework. KUMP introduces two key innovations: eText-masked Image Pretraining (eMIP) and eText-guided Image Decoding (eTID). During eMIP, models are trained to reconstruct masked portions of eText within images, thereby enforcing a strong alignment between visual and textual signals. Furthermore, eTID enhances this representation by enabling the model to reconstruct the complete original eText from the masked images it has repaired. Extensive experiments across eText classification, image search, and recommendation tasks demonstrate that KUMP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Our source code can be accessed at https://github.com/THUIAM/KUMP.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent and fatal neurodegenerative condition that typically begins with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) before advancing to the severe stage of AD. The transition from MCI to AD represents a critical clinical progression, and identifying the risk factors associated with this advance could enable the development of preventative therapies. This study introduces the application of the Deep InfoMax (DIM) architecture to predict MCI conversion using electronic health record (EHR) data. DIM functions as a self-supervised model that learns to differentiate between genuine and spurious correlations within data. We evaluated the model on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset, which includes longitudinal MRI scans and clinical assessments for subjects with AD, MCI, and healthy controls. The data were partitioned into distinct cohorts: 424 AD patients, 678 MCI patients, and 694 healthy controls. Our results indicate that the DIM model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.866 in predicting MCI progression to AD. These findings suggest that DIM offers a robust method for leveraging clinical and radiological features from EHRs to forecast AD progression.

Comprehending the meaning of a text relies on the continuous integration of a language model's internal state with semantic details as the input is processed. However, current methods struggle to effectively address this challenge. This study introduces a new L-shaped architecture, termed L-Net, specifically designed to enhance the model's ability to understand its own language semantics. By employing an attention mechanism, L-Net facilitates a continuous interaction between a question and the evolving internal language model state. This interaction enables the model to access contextual information from prior words when determining meanings for current ones. Additionally, an attention-driven mechanism highlights specific words in the input text that are most relevant to a query, thereby enriching the semantic details available to the model. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the capability to discern word meanings in context.

We investigate the influence of strong electron correlations within a $d$-orbital framework featuring easy-plane spin-anisotropy and spin-orbit coupling. Starting with a multi-orbital model subjected to strong spin-orbit interactions, we employ the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to compute the self-energy, subsequently determining the ground state and characteristic energy scales. The study reveals that correlations significantly amplify the effective spin-orbit coupling, generating a self-energy component that scales with the square of the spin-orbit interaction strength multiplied by the imaginary part of the optical conductivity. Consequently, this enhancement can drive a metal-insulator transition. Furthermore, our analysis identifies two distinct regimes of effective coupling: at low temperatures, the interaction strength is governed by the ratio between spin-orbit coupling and bandwidth, whereas at high temperatures, correlations dominate through the ratio of spin-orbit coupling to the energy gap in the single-particle excitation spectrum.

We propose a new dark matter candidate known as Shadow Matter, which interacts with the Standard Model exclusively through the Higgs portal. This mechanism allows a non-zero mixing between the Standard Model's conformal sector and itself, enabling freeze-in production processes. In this scenario, shadow matter exists in a metastable state relative to the conformal sector and possesses mass in the GeV–TeV range. This setup is consistent with current direct and indirect detection limits, offering a viable explanation for the excess signals observed by the LUX experiment and by gamma-ray observatories such as Fermi-LAT and HESS. Furthermore, this framework provides a compelling explanation for the origin of neutrino masses.

Regulatory bodies mandate that medical device manufacturers validate and verify their software using rigorous testing, especially when a test dataset differs from the system's operational environment. For artificial intelligence (AI) driven systems, this requirement poses a significant challenge because conventional software verification techniques struggle to establish the reliability of machine learning models. We propose a testing framework that leverages a black-box algorithm to formally verify a conformer prediction framework for AI medical devices. By utilizing methods that account for distribution shifts, our approach demonstrates how to reliably estimate AI model performance with statistical confidence, even when a held-out test set differs from the training environment.

This study introduces the utilization of biasing potentials in molecular simulations to model the bending of long DNA strands anchored to a rigid surface. We demonstrate that clamping one end of the DNA to a fixed boundary significantly accelerates the exploration of the DNA's energy landscape, facilitating the capture of physically significant conformations that are difficult to achieve through standard sampling alone. This computational approach is validated experimentally by comparing the resulting structures with data from cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Our findings indicate that this technique successfully reproduces the observed length-dependent increase in DNA curvature, thereby offering a novel strategy for capturing specific conformational states essential for subsequent applications in drug design.

This study examines an underappreciated compression technique called Ans, which operates by modeling the probability of the preceding character to encode the current one. We present a novel algorithmic approach to building Ans trees that achieves superior compression performance. Additionally, we introduce a method for parallelizing the Ans compression process, significantly reducing runtime. Comprehensive tests on various benchmarks demonstrate that our compressed outputs are notably smaller than those produced by existing implementations, while also reducing compression time by a factor of several hundred. To further validate our approach, we conducted extensive trials on real-world datasets, including genomic sequences and social network data, where our method similarly outperformed competitors in both compression ratios and speed.

Measuring dielectric permittivity via the frequency range of 1 MHz to 1 GHz enables the detection of moisture and ion concentrations in cement-based materials. This technique is non-destructive and facilitates the non-invasive assessment of pore fluid composition and fluid distribution within such materials. This study examines the dielectric behavior of pore solutions in cement-based materials, specifically focusing on calcium chloride and sodium chloride solutions alongside pure water. The analysis involves comparing experimental results with the mixing rules proposed by Bruggeman and the Debye polarization model. The findings indicate that the mixing rules are applicable only to pore solutions containing low salt concentrations. Furthermore, the pore solution's dielectric behavior is characterized by a single relaxation time derived from the Debye model, a parameter that increases with the inclusion of salt. Additionally, the relaxation frequency for pure water is noted to be approximately 1000 times greater than the relaxation frequency of a saturated salt solution. This research offers a foundational understanding of the dielectric characteristics of pore solutions, serving as a critical prerequisite for the effective application of ground penetrating radar in cement-based material analysis.

This review examines hadronic molecules composed of heavy hadrons, focusing on those where at least two particles are massive, and analyzes the distinctive characteristics of their spectrum and binding mechanisms. We begin by outlining the unique dynamics of heavy-heavy hadron systems, such as the $DD^*$ and $DN$ channels, demonstrating how these properties facilitate molecular formation. The text then presents a detailed analysis of the $D_D^*$ molecule, highlighting its binding energy and mass spectrum. Furthermore, we discuss the possibility of forming $D D^*$ molecules in an excited P-wave state. In the concluding section, we outline the distinctive features of $D D^*$ systems and propose directions for future research.

This paper outlines a natural language processing (NLP)-based approach to analyzing the development drivers of autonomous swarm robotics for military applications. The study begins by contextualizing swarm robotics within military uses, followed by a detailed examination of the specific evolution factors shaping this field. It is further argued that deriving insights from existing academic literature could significantly benefit researchers and engineers working on similar systems. Consequently, a methodology employing NLP techniques to investigate these military development factors is presented.

We introduce a technique to directly and model-freely derive cosmological parameters from the three-dimensional correlations of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest pixels. This method relies on the assumption that Lyman forest pixels act as unbiased tracers of the dark matter distribution. We present the functional form of these parameters in a model-independent way using the three-point correlation function of Lyman forest pixels. We apply this method to the SDSS-III Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) data and calculate the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the angular diameter distance to the Lyman forest ($D_A$) at redshift $z=2.34$. We find $H_0 = 67.6 \pm 1.1$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and $D_A = 1650 \pm 140$ Mpc. These results are consistent with the Planck 2015 cosmological model but exhibit a $2.6\sigma$ discrepancy with the Planck value for $D_A$ at $z=2.34$.

Emittance serves as a critical metric for characterizing the quality of a particle accelerator beam. Emitters can be categorized into either horizontal or vertical (transverse) components, as well as longitudinal ones. Emittance transfer, a process where one type of emittance is converted into another, has previously been theorized but not directly observed. This study reports the first experimental confirmation of such transfer between trans and longitudinal emission. Emittance transfer, a phenomenon theoretically predicted, has now been confirmed for the first time in this study. It involves the conversion of one type of particle beam emission into another, a process not observed before. This significant breakthrough confirms the theoretical predictions made earlier.

This paper introduces a new trajectory prediction framework designed to generate diverse and socially compliant future paths for traffic agents. Unlike many existing approaches that rely on independent learning of behavior patterns, this method generates plausible trajectories by capturing the interdependencies among multiple vehicles. Specifically, it employs the Socially Aware Reinforcement Learning (SARL) framework, which is built upon a sequential latent variable model. This model utilizes successive latent representations derived from the CVAE architecture to capture temporal dynamics in driving actions. To enhance prediction diversity, the system employs a sliding inference mechanism that processes the recent trajectory history of all surrounding vehicles. Additionally, a novel reward structure has been created to evaluate and refine the agents' social compliance at every time step. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of diversity and social compliance metrics.

The capacity to model complex probability distributions using networks of interconnected units is a central challenge in machine learning. While the Boltzmann machine serves as a foundational framework for understanding complex correlations, its application is often hindered by training difficulties and scalability issues. This study investigates methods to mitigate these challenges by reducing network complexity through the elimination of redundant or unnecessary connections. We analyze various sparsification techniques and assess their impact on both probability distribution approximation capabilities and inference efficiency. To evaluate overall complexity, we employ multiple information-theoretic metrics and measure learning performance using three distinct metrics of learning error alongside inference time on a simplified model of learning to predict coin toss outcomes. Our results demonstrate that several of the proposed methods maintain high approximation capabilities while substantially lowering complexity, thereby offering more efficient routes toward effective models suitable for real-world tasks.

With the advent of high-performance computing and advances in swarm robotics, we are entering an era where humans can interact with and manage large groups of robots. While Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) is typically reserved for specific tasks under human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop supervision, this study addresses a different scenario: Decentralized Human-Swarm Interaction (HSSI). In HSSI, individuals can independently control autonomous robot swarms without direct operational oversight. To demonstrate this, we developed a system enabling users to guide a robot swarm autonomously using a series of hand gestures. This approach relies on a sequential learning system that leverages the distinct characteristics of different gestures to encode specific commands. The system's performance was evaluated in two settings: a simulation involving the sequential execution of four tasks and a physical experiment where the gestures directed a real Khepera III robot in performing five sequential tasks.

Automatically classifying blood cells is a critical diagnostic tool for identifying various disorders, including leukemia and anemia. This study introduces two novel deep learning architectures, CPAM and PCEM, which integrate convolutional and fully connected neural networks to achieve outstanding performance. The CPAM model consists of a 6-layer convolutional network and a 7-layer neural network, while PCEM features 5 convolutional and 8 neural layers respectively. Both models utilize a Softmax output layer for automatic classification. Evaluated on the publicly available "Blood MNIST" dataset, these models were compared against other deep learning approaches, including Lenet-5, AlexNet, LeNet, VGG-16, VGG-17, ResNet-18, and DenseNet-17. Testing results indicate that PCEM and CPAM significantly outperform these baselines, with both achieving an accuracy rate of 99.99% and an F1 score of 99.99%, compared to the top-performing models like ResNet-D17 and VGG-D17, which achieved 99.99% and an F1 score of 99.99%, respectively.

Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols are powerful techniques for rapidly preparing ground states, yet the feasibility of implementing counteriagical terms in real-world systems is often hindered by the complexity of adding counteriagical degrees of freedom. In this work, we introduce a novel strategy to construct CD terms for the one-dimensional Hubbard model, demonstrating that it allows for the fast initialization of the Hubbard model's ground state using solely two auxiliary qubits. The performance of our method is validated through variational optimization, and numerical simulations indicate that the protocol achieves near-perfect fidelity ($\mathcal{F} \approx 1$) even at high temperatures ($k_B T \approx 0.1 J$) and despite noise.

This work presents a proposed solution for detecting and quantifying discoloration in images. The primary challenge lies in accurately identifying and measuring the temperature of these chromatic variations. The proposed methodology employs a novel, rapid technique to determine the color temperature of a given white point. The validity of this approach was verified through experiments comparing it against an established K-means clustering method. The findings indicate that the new technique is highly effective, as its accuracy closely mirrors that of the reference K-means algorithm. Additionally, the system's performance was evaluated in the context of tone mapping. The results demonstrate that utilizing this method for identifying and isolating the warm areas of an image yields superior outcomes compared to traditional techniques.

"This paper introduces the Exponential Taylor Expansion, a technique for precisely and efficiently transforming functions involving exponentials into optimized forms of polynomial approximations. The method integrates partial remainder management with an optimized table-lookup strategy to achieve high numerical accuracy while maintaining computational speed comparable to that of the standard Taylor series approach.

Let $M$ be a metric sphere equipped with $\text{CAT}(m)$ geometry and dimension $n \geq 2$, and let $\pi: \Sigma \to M$ be a branched covering map originating from a Riemann surface $\Sigma$. This work demonstrates that if the harmonic map $\pi$ possesses a non-empty branch set, a map $\pi$ cannot exist. Consequently, we derive that any branched covering $\pi: \Sigma \to S^n$ mapping from a Riemann surface to a sphere of dimension $n \geq 2$ must be unbranched (a holomorphic covering), a result that resolves the case $n \geq 2$ of the Uniformization Theorem for branched coverings.

Laser-plasma interactions represent a potent method for generating high-flux photon beams, which can subsequently collide with one another to reveal relativistic photon-photon phenomena. This work introduces a comprehensive laser-plasma framework designed to model the generation of these colliding beams and assess their suitability for detecting such interactions. Specifically, we examine beam production mechanisms within a one-dimensional plasma model that accounts for radiative reaction effects. This analysis provides a means to quantify beam characteristics and define optimal operational plasma regimes for facilitating robust photon-photon collisions.

This paper examines the sensitivity of the 2HDM model, specifically regarding the soft $Z_2$ breaking parameter $m_{12}$, by analyzing its impact on the predicted Higgs masses. We evaluate this sensitivity across the three primary Higgs boson categories—$h$, $H$, and $A$—using the current experimental data available. We conclude by discussing the specific constraints and limitations inherent in the $m_{12}$ parameter within the context of the Higgs mass spectrum.

While Relational To RDF (R2RDF) mappings enable the conversion of databases into RDF, integrating shape-based schema (such as Shapes Constraint Language - SHACL) into this process presents specific challenges. Shapes provide a flexible mechanism for defining graph structure constraints, yet mapping relations to these shapes often results in semantic gaps or redundancies. To address this, a mapping framework is proposed that automatically generates corresponding shape definitions for relational data structures. This approach is grounded in the ShEx language and utilizes the Cypher query language to specify the integration logic between relational databases and shape-based schemas. The proposed solution demonstrates its effectiveness through a practical application featuring a tourism information service.

This article introduces pyStoNED, a flexible and user-friendly Python package designed for convex regression and frontier estimation. While focused on convex regression, the tool also supports a range of non-parametric frontier estimation methods, including MND, Gamma-MNED, MNED, and production TED. Written in an user-centric style, the paper details the internal architecture of pyStoNED and demonstrates its capabilities through two applied case studies. The first examines the relationship between COVID-19 mortality rates and advancing age, while a subsequent analysis explores firm-level total factor productivity within the Spanish manufacturing sector, illustrating both output-oriented and input-oriented production efficiency. To facilitate easy adoption, the authors provide supplementary Python notebooks that accompany the examples and enable readers to replicate all analyses and code demonstrations presented herein.

We present a method for detecting the SM-like Higgs boson ($\phi$) within the context of the SM-like Higgs doublet plus a singlet (LHC) framework, specifically through the $t \bar t \phi$ process. This approach involves examining the kinematic spectrum of top quarks, which exhibits a characteristic shape that enables the discrimination of this model from the Standard Model. This analysis relies on the $\Gamma_{\rm PS}$ variable, derived from Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs), to probe production mechanisms. We utilize NNLO-in-$\phi$ QCD calculations to ensure precision. This theoretical framework is then applied to LHC data collected at 13 TeV, yielding constraints on the relevant Lagrangian parameters.

We introduce a straightforward technique for utilizing unsupervised or few-shot tasks derived from pretrained language models. This method involves generating contextualized tokens by replacing a target class label in an entity description with its class name during the training of models like BERT. Consequently, the context surrounding an entity is filled by substituting its class name into the blank. We demonstrate that this approach allows for ranker generation through few-shot tasks or even unsupervised settings by using the resulting fill-in-the-blank architecture to produce effective search query auto-completion results.

Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is a critical component of automated telephone systems. While Deep Learning approaches have largely replaced rule-based methods for ITN, they frequently require vast amounts of manually annotated data, which is often scarce. To address this data bottleneck, our study investigates data augmentation as a strategy to increase available training samples. Our results demonstrate that models leveraging this augmented data achieve superior performance compared to those trained under standard conditions.

This research establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the principal eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator under Robin boundary conditions. Additionally, the eigen-optimal domain and the entire set of energy-optimal sets are identified. As direct consequences, the first eigen-function associated with the Hermitiean operator, subjected to Robin constraints on a star-shaped domain, exhibits strict monotonicity along each radial direction.

Kernel methods serve as a powerful non-parametric approach for constructing kernels on manifolds, yet they struggle with non-compact spaces due to reliance on positive definiteness. To address this, we introduce a new kernel class termed "Tangential Kernels," which permit extensions beyond compact manifolds. These kernels are built from an underlying Eucentric kernel using a positive-definite base kernel as an auxiliary; this construction yields two key properties: a guaranteed spectral bound relative to the auxiliary helper and a guaranteed positive semidefinite nature. Since they behave similarly to standard kernels, existing kernel-based algorithms can be readily adapted for use. We provide a rigorous proof for their positivity (in the generalized sense) and establish their relationship to the standard Eucentric kernel. Additionally, we validate their practicality by testing them on conventional datasets and datasets containing holes.

We introduce a new task for synthetic speech focused on creating socially diverse characters through specific vocal features, including volume, pitch, and speech rate. We examine the challenges of aligning social characteristics with speech output and present a new dataset comprising 1,000 distinct synthetic personas, each with 10 variations of audio. Additionally, we introduce a classification model capable of identifying a speaker's persona and a transduction system that modifies a speaker's personality while preserving their voice quality. Experiments confirm that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the target tasks.

We introduce a radiative seesaw model featuring a light fermionic dark matter candidate, structured around $U(1)_{B-L}$ and modular $A_4$ symmetries. Leveraging modular invariance, neutrino mass generation is achieved through the mechanism of radiative loops. Our analysis reveals that a dark matter mass falling within the GeV–TeV regime can evade current direct and indirect detection limits.

The influence of the minimum length on collective dynamics within triaxial nuclei is examined using a Bohr-Landau Hamiltonian framework. In this study, triaxial collectivity is modeled as a combination of oscillations along the $z$-axis and rotational motion around the same axis, subject to a minimum length constraint along that $z$-direction. Consequently, the potential energy function is modified to account for this constraint, and the resulting triaxial collective Hamiltonian is derived. Rotational spectra generated from this modified Hamiltonian are then compared with those of a conventional system lacking a minimum length, as well as with available experimental data for the triaxial nucleus $^{166}\text{Er}$. The analysis reveals that incorporating the minimum length leads to a reduction in calculated moments of inertia relative to standard models, while the magnitude of this decrease is found to be negligible when contrasted with existing experimental uncertainties.
